Supervisory oversight: the RBI’s Department of Supervision conducts thematic inspections on outsourcing risk. In the 2023‑24 cycle, 7 banks were penalised a total of ₹3.1 crore for breaching the 30 % single‑provider limit and for insufficient exit‑strategy documentation. The guidelines also require REs to maintain a “Vendor Risk Register” updated quarterly and to submit an annual attestation of compliance to the RBI.

The framework aligns with the Basel Committee’s “Principles for Outsourcing” and the Financial Stability Board’s “Guidance on Cloud Concentration Risk”. It reflects the RBI’s shift from a rules‑based to a principles‑based supervisory approach, emphasising board‑level ownership of third‑party risk.

Cyber Resilience Framework, Incident Reporting and the Cyber Risk Rating

The RBI’s “Cyber Security Framework for Banks” (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2021‑22) and the subsequent “Cyber Risk Rating (CRR) Methodology” (2023) constitute the cornerstone of supervisory expectations for cyber resilience. The framework mandates: (i) a board‑approved Cyber Security Policy reviewed annually; (ii) a dedicated Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) reporting directly to the board; (iii) implementation of the “Zero Trust” architecture for all critical systems; (iv) mandatory participation in the RBI‑run “Cyber Security Drills” (quarterly tabletop exercises and annual red‑team simulations).

Incident‑reporting obligations: REs must notify the RBI’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT‑RBI) within 6 hours of detecting a cyber incident that affects confidentiality, integrity or availability of critical data or services. A detailed root‑cause analysis and remediation plan must be submitted within 15 days. Failure to report attracts a penalty of up to ₹1 crore per incident under the Banking Regulation Act.

The CRR, introduced in 2023, assigns each RE a rating from 1 (lowest risk) to 5 (highest risk) based on 42 quantitative and qualitative indicators — including patch‑management latency, privileged‑access controls, third‑party risk scores, and drill performance. The rating is not publicly disclosed; it is shared only with the supervised entity and feeds into the Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP) score. In the 2023‑24 SREP cycle, 12 banks received a CRR of 4 or 5, triggering enhanced supervisory engagement and a requirement to submit a time‑bound Cyber Resilience Improvement Plan.

The RBI also issued “Guidelines on Cyber Security for Payment System Operators” (2022) extending similar obligations to NPCI, card networks, and PPI issuers. The 2024 Financial Stability Report noted a 34 % reduction in high‑severity incidents across the banking sector after the CRR became a supervisory input, underscoring the effectiveness of a risk‑based rating coupled with mandatory drills.

  • Confusing the 30 % single‑provider cloud limit with a blanket cap on all IT assets; the limit applies only to critical workloads.
  • Assuming the Digital Lending Guidelines impose an interest‑rate ceiling; they require only all‑in‑cost transparency.
  • Believing the co‑lending model permits the NBFC to hold the entire loan off the bank’s balance sheet; the bank must retain at least 10‑20 % on its books.
  • Treating the Cyber Risk Rating as a public disclosure; it is confidential and used solely for supervisory action.
  • Overlooking that the 180‑day remediation window for existing cloud contracts started on 30 April 2023, not from the circular date.
  • Thinking the cooling‑off period under the Digital Lending Guidelines is uniform; it varies by ticket size (3 days ≤ ₹5 lakh, 7 days > ₹5 lakh).
  • Assuming the outsourcing framework exempts non‑critical workloads from audit‑right clauses; all contracts must contain audit rights regardless of criticality.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market and the RBI's Market Making Operations

The corporate bond market in India has historically been shallow, with limited secondary‑market liquidity and a narrow investor base dominated by banks and mutual funds. Monetary policy influences this segment through three primary channels: the interest‑rate channel, the credit‑spread channel, and the liquidity channel. When the policy repo rate moves, the risk‑free yield curve shifts, altering the discount rate for all fixed‑income securities. Simultaneously, changes in systemic liquidity affect the willingness of market participants to hold lower‑rated paper, widening or compressing credit spreads. The RBI has complemented these indirect effects with direct market‑making interventions.

In March 2020 the RBI announced a Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) with an initial allocation of ₹1 lakh crore to stabilise the market during the pandemic‑induced sell‑off. The programme operated through primary dealers who were mandated to quote two‑way prices for a defined basket of investment‑grade corporate bonds. Purchases were settled on a delivery‑versus‑payment basis via the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL), ensuring settlement finality. The CBPP was later extended and its size adjusted in line with evolving liquidity conditions, signalling the central bank’s commitment to prevent a disorderly freeze.

Beyond outright purchases, the RBI introduced a triparty repo platform for corporate bonds in 2021, allowing banks and primary dealers to borrow against high‑quality corporate paper at rates close to the policy repo. This facility deepened the repo market, reduced haircut volatility, and provided an additional liquidity backstop for mutual funds facing redemption pressures. The central bank also prescribed market‑making obligations for primary dealers: each dealer must maintain continuous bid‑ask quotes for at least 30 specified corporate bonds, with a maximum spread of 15 basis points for AAA‑rated issues and 30 basis points for AA‑rated issues. Compliance is monitored through daily reporting to the RBI’s Market Operations Department.

Empirical evidence from the 2020‑22 period shows that the CBPP and the repo facility compressed credit spreads by 40‑60 basis points for AAA issuers and by 80‑120 basis points for AA issuers, while secondary‑market turnover rose by roughly 35 per cent. The transmission to new issuance was evident in the decline of coupon rates on fresh AAA paper by 25‑35 basis points relative to the pre‑programme benchmark. However, the impact on lower‑rated and unrated segments remained muted, reflecting persistent information asymmetry and the absence of a comparable backstop.

Going forward, the RBI’s focus is on institutionalising a standing corporate bond market‑making framework, integrating the repo platform with the forthcoming Central Counterparty (CCP) for corporate bonds, and encouraging participation from insurance companies and pension funds through regulatory incentives. These steps aim to make the corporate bond market a more reliable conduit for monetary policy transmission, reducing the economy’s over‑reliance on bank credit.

RBI's Variable Rate Repo Operations and Their Effect on the Overnight Indexed Swap Curve

The Reserve Bank of India transitioned from a fixed‑rate liquidity framework to an auction‑based variable‑rate regime in 2022 with the introduction of Variable Rate Repo (VRR) and Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) operations. Under VRR, the RBI injects liquidity by conducting repo auctions where the cut‑off rate is discovered through competitive bidding; under VRRR it absorbs surplus liquidity via reverse‑repo auctions. Both instruments operate with tenors ranging from overnight to 14 days and are announced on a daily basis, giving the central bank fine‑grained control over the quantum and price of short‑term funds.

The VRR cut‑off rate typically tracks the policy repo rate within a narrow band, because banks bid up to the marginal cost of funds they can deploy in the market. When systemic liquidity is abundant, the VRR cut‑off may trade a few basis points below the repo rate; during tight conditions it can exceed the repo rate, signalling stress. The VRRR cut‑off, conversely, anchors the floor of the interest‑rate corridor, replacing the erstwhile fixed reverse‑repo rate. The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) provides an additional floor at a fixed rate, but the VRRR remains the primary tool for active liquidity absorption.

These auction outcomes feed directly into the Overnight Indexed Swap (OIS) curve, which reflects market expectations of the average overnight rate over various horizons. The 1‑month and 3‑month OIS rates are particularly sensitive to the VRR/VRRR cut‑offs because they are constructed from compounded overnight rates. When the VRR cut‑off rises, the short end of the OIS curve steepens, signalling tighter future policy expectations. Conversely, a lower VRRR cut‑off flattens the curve. Market participants use the OIS curve to price interest‑rate derivatives, hedge floating‑rate exposures, and gauge the stance of monetary policy beyond the headline repo rate.

The RBI publishes the weighted average cut‑off rates and the total allotted amount for each auction, providing transparency that reduces uncertainty. In the 2023‑24 financial year, the VRR auction size averaged ₹2.5 lakh crore per day, while VRRR absorption averaged ₹1.8 lakh crore, indicating a net injection stance consistent with the accommodative policy posture. The OIS curve responded with a 10‑15 basis point upward shift in the 1‑month tenor during periods of net absorption, and a comparable downward shift during net injection phases.

Operationally, the variable‑rate framework enhances the RBI’s ability to manage liquidity shocks — such as advance tax outflows or government cash‑balance swings — without resorting to ad‑hoc open‑market operations. It also improves the signalling channel: the auction cut‑off becomes a high‑frequency indicator of the central bank’s liquidity preference, complementing the forward guidance communicated through the Monetary Policy Committee minutes. For banks, the predictable auction calendar facilitates better asset‑liability management and reduces the need for costly overnight borrowing from the marginal standing facility.

Worked Example
A bank observes that the 1‑month OIS rate has risen 12 basis points above the policy repo rate while the VRR cut‑off is trading 5 basis points above the repo rate. Explain the likely liquidity condition and the bank’s optimal short‑term funding strategy.
The rise in the 1‑month OIS above the repo rate indicates that market participants expect the average overnight rate to be higher than the current policy rate over the next month, implying a tightening bias. The VRR cut‑off trading above the repo rate confirms that banks are willing to pay a premium for liquidity, signalling a deficit in the system. In this environment the bank should avoid relying on the marginal standing facility (which carries a penalty rate) and instead participate in the VRR auctions to secure funds at the market‑determined cut‑off. Simultaneously, the bank can enter into pay‑fixed OIS contracts to lock in the current elevated swap rate, hedging the risk of further increases in its cost of funds. If the bank holds excess government securities, it can also use the triparty repo platform to borrow against them at rates close to the VRR cut‑off, which is cheaper than the MSF. The combined strategy minimises funding cost while providing certainty over the near‑term interest‑rate outlook.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question links VRR/VRRR cut‑offs to the OIS curve, first identify the direction of the liquidity shock (injection vs absorption). Then trace the impact: injection → lower VRR cut‑off → lower short‑end OIS; absorption → higher VRRR cut‑off → higher short‑end OIS. Use the interest‑rate corridor diagram (repo → VRR → SDF → VRRR) to visualise the floor and ceiling. Mention the daily auction calendar and the publication of weighted average rates as transparency mechanisms that reduce term‑premium volatility.

Macroprudential Oversight of Systemically Important Financial Market Infrastructures: Central Counterparties and Settlement Systems

Financial market infrastructures (FMIs) such as central counterparties (CCPs) and large‑value payment systems constitute the plumbing of the financial system. Their failure can transmit shocks across markets instantaneously, making macroprudential oversight essential. The RBI, in line with the CPMI‑IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (PFMI), has established a dedicated supervisory framework for CCPs and designated systemically important payment systems (SIPS).

The Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL) is the primary CCP for the rupee‑denominated government securities, foreign‑exchange, and money‑market segments. The National Securities Clearing Corporation Ltd (NSCCL) clears equity and equity‑derivative trades. Both entities are subject to the RBI’s 2020 “Guidelines for Central Counterparties”, which prescribe minimum capital requirements (₹300 crore for CCIL, ₹250 crore for NSCCL), daily margin modelling based on historical value‑at‑risk with a 99 per cent confidence interval over a 10‑day horizon, and a default fund sized to cover the failure of the two largest clearing members under extreme but plausible stress scenarios. The guidelines also mandate segregation of client assets, real‑time position monitoring, and a recovery plan approved by the board.

In 2021 the RBI issued the “Framework for Systemically Important Payment Systems”, designating RTGS, NEFT, and UPI as SIPS. These systems must maintain a minimum net‑worth of ₹500 crore, conduct annual business‑continuity drills, and submit quarterly operational‑risk reports. The framework requires interoperability standards — for instance, UPI’s common‑library specification ensures that any bank or payment‑service provider can connect without bilateral agreements. Settlement finality is legally enshrined under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, which provides that a settlement instruction is irrevocable once accepted by the system operator.

Supervisory intensity is calibrated through a risk‑based rating: CCPs and SIPS are assigned a supervisory category (1 to 4) based on capital adequacy, margin‑model robustness, cyber‑resilience, and governance. Entities in categories 3 and 4 face enhanced on‑site inspections, mandatory external audits of margin models, and a requirement to submit a time‑bound remediation plan. In the 2023‑24 supervisory cycle, CCIL was placed in category 2, reflecting adequate capital but a need to strengthen its default‑fund stress‑testing methodology. NSCCL received a category 1 rating, benefiting from its diversified clearing‑member base and advanced margin models.

The macroprudential payoff of this architecture is evident in the resilience displayed during the March 2020 market turbulence. CCIL’s margin calls were met without disruption, and the default fund was not tapped. UPI processed a record 2.7 billion transactions in a single month in 2023 with a settlement‑failure rate below 0.001 per cent. Ongoing work includes the integration of a CCP for corporate bonds, the adoption of a common‑risk‑management platform for all FMIs, and the alignment of Indian standards with the forthcoming G20‑endorsed “Cross‑Border Payment” roadmap.

Retail Central Bank Digital Currency Pilot: Offline Token Design, Interoperability with UPI, and Merchant Adoption

The RBI launched the retail Central Bank Digital Currency pilot (e₹‑R) in December 2022, initially covering four cities — Mumbai, New Delhi, Bengaluru, and Bhubaneswar — and expanding to 15 cities by March 2024. The pilot uses a token‑based, bearer instrument model where each digital rupee token represents a claim on the central bank and carries no interest. Tokens are issued in denominations mirroring physical currency (₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200, ₹500) and are stored in a digital wallet provided by participating banks.

A distinguishing feature is offline capability. The wallet application supports Near‑Field Communication (NFC) and QR‑code based peer‑to‑peer transfers without an active internet connection. Offline transactions are cryptographically signed on the device and later synchronised with the RBI’s ledger when connectivity is restored. To limit counter‑party risk, the RBI caps offline transfers at ₹2,000 per transaction and ₹10,000 per day per wallet. These limits are enforced by the wallet software and verified during the next online sync.

Interoperability with the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) is achieved through a “UPI‑CBDC bridge” operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). Users can link their CBDC wallet to a UPI ID, enabling instant transfer of funds between the CBDC wallet and any UPI‑enabled bank account. The bridge settles on a gross‑settlement basis in real time, preserving the finality of both systems. Merchants benefit because they can accept e₹‑R via the same QR code used for UPI payments; the merchant’s acquirer routes the transaction through the bridge, crediting the merchant’s bank account in rupees while debiting the customer’s CBDC wallet.

Merchant adoption has been encouraged through a zero‑merchant‑discount‑rate (MDR) policy for CBDC transactions during the pilot phase, and by onboarding kirana stores through bank‑led outreach programmes. As of the latest pilot review, over 1.2 lakh merchants across the 15 cities accept e₹‑R, and daily transaction volumes have crossed 250,000, with an average ticket size of ₹180. The RBI monitors usage metrics — wallet activation rate, offline‑sync success ratio, and fraud incidents — through a dedicated dashboard. Early data show an offline‑sync success ratio above 99.5 per cent and a fraud rate of less than 0.02 per cent of transaction value.

Key challenges remain: user education on wallet security, the need for a robust dispute‑resolution mechanism for offline transactions, and the scalability of the token‑ledger architecture to handle nationwide volumes. The RBI has indicated that a phased nationwide rollout will follow a comprehensive impact assessment, with particular attention to financial‑inclusion outcomes in rural and semi‑urban areas where smartphone penetration is lower.

RBI's Supervisory Framework for Large Exposure and Concentration Risk in Non‑Bank Financial Companies

While the large‑exposure framework for commercial banks was tightened in 2023, the RBI extended a comparable regime to Non‑Bank Financial Companies (NBFCs) classified in the Upper Layer (NBFC‑UL) under the Scale‑Based Regulation introduced in 2021. The 2023 “Large Exposure and Concentration Risk Guidelines for NBFC‑UL” set explicit caps: exposure to a single counterparty (or a group of connected counterparties) must not exceed 20 per cent of the NBFC’s Tier I capital; aggregate exposure to a group of connected counterparties must not exceed 25 per cent of Tier I capital. These limits apply to both on‑balance‑sheet and off‑balance‑sheet items, including guarantees, derivatives, and committed credit lines.

The framework requires NBFC‑ULs to compute exposures on a gross basis, without netting of collateral, except for eligible financial collateral that meets the RBI’s haircut schedule. Concentration risk is monitored through a quarterly “Large Exposure Return” submitted to the Department of Supervision. The return captures counterparty‑wise exposure, sectoral distribution, and the credit‑rating profile of large borrowers. NBFCs breaching the limits must submit a board‑approved remediation plan within 30 days and reduce the excess exposure within 180 days. Persistent non‑compliance attracts supervisory actions ranging from restriction on fresh lending to the imposition of additional capital charges.

Sectoral concentration is addressed through a supplementary guideline: exposure to the real‑estate sector (including construction finance) must not exceed 30 per cent of the NBFC’s total loan book, and exposure to the capital‑market segment (margin funding, loan against shares) is capped at 15 per cent. These sectoral caps are calibrated to the historical default experience of NBFC‑ULs during the 2018‑19 liquidity stress. The RBI also mandates a quarterly stress‑test of the large‑exposure portfolio under a scenario of a 200‑basis‑point rise in interest rates combined with a 15‑per‑cent decline in collateral values.

Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) in the Upper Layer are subject to an analogous regime, with an additional requirement that the loan‑to‑value (LTV) ratio on individual housing loans does not exceed 80 per cent for loans above ₹75 lakh. The HFC‑specific norms also require a minimum 10 per cent risk‑weight on loans to developers, reflecting the higher granularity risk in project finance.

The impact of these measures is visible in the declining share of large‑exposure breaches: from 12 NBFC‑ULs reporting excess exposures in the March 2022 quarter to only 3 in the March 2024 quarter. The framework has also incentivised NBFCs to diversify funding sources, with a noticeable shift toward securitisation and co‑lending arrangements that keep individual exposures within limits while expanding overall credit supply.

  • Confusing the CBPP with the corporate bond repo facility; the former is outright purchase, the latter is collateralised lending.
  • Assuming the VRR cut‑off always equals the policy repo rate; it can trade above or below depending on liquidity conditions.
  • Treating CCIL and NSCCL as subject to identical capital requirements; CCIL requires ₹300 crore, NSCCL ₹250 crore.
  • Believing offline CBDC transactions have no limits; they are capped at ₹2,000 per transaction and ₹10,000 daily.
  • Thinking the large‑exposure caps for NBFC‑ULs apply on a net‑collateral basis; they are gross‑exposure limits with limited collateral netting.
  • Overlooking that the UPI‑CBDC bridge settles on a gross‑settlement basis, not a deferred net‑settlement basis.
  • Assuming the sectoral concentration caps for NBFCs are uniform across all sectors; real‑estate and capital‑market segments have distinct limits.

Domestic Systemically Important Banks: Assessment Methodology and Enhanced Supervision

The Reserve Bank of India adopted the Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIB) framework in July 2014, aligning with the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) methodology while calibrating thresholds to the Indian banking structure. The framework mandates that banks identified as D-SIBs hold additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital surcharges, applied as an extension of the capital conservation buffer, to internalise the negative externalities their failure would impose on the domestic financial system and the real economy.

The assessment methodology follows a two-step process. First, a sample of banks is selected based on size: any bank having a Basel III leverage ratio exposure measure exceeding 2 per cent of GDP is automatically included. Second, the selected banks are scored on four indicators — size, interconnectedness, substitutability, and complexity — each carrying equal weight. The composite systemic importance score determines the bucket in which the bank is placed. The RBI reviews the list annually, using end-March data, and announces the outcome typically in August or September.

As of the March 2024 assessment, three banks remain designated as D-SIBs: State Bank of India (SBI) in bucket 3 (requiring a 0.60 per cent CET1 surcharge), and ICICI Bank and HDFC Bank in bucket 1 (requiring a 0.20 per cent CET1 surcharge). The bucketing structure has five buckets (1 to 5) with surcharges rising in steps of 0.20 per cent; bucket 5 carries a 1.00 per cent surcharge. No Indian bank has yet been placed in buckets 2, 4, or 5. The surcharge must be met entirely with CET1 capital and is phased in over the same timeline as the capital conservation buffer.

Beyond capital, D-SIBs are subject to enhanced supervisory intensity. They undergo more frequent and deeper supervisory engagements, including dedicated on-site inspections, thematic reviews of risk governance, and mandatory recovery and resolution planning. Each D-SIB must submit a recovery plan annually, detailing credible options to restore financial strength under severe stress, and a resolution plan (living will) providing the resolution authority with information to facilitate orderly resolution. The RBI also requires D-SIBs to maintain a higher level of disclosure under Pillar 3, including granular data on cross-border exposures, intra-group transactions, and concentration risk.

The 2022 review of the D-SIB framework introduced two refinements. The leverage ratio exposure measure replaced total assets as the size indicator, improving comparability across accounting regimes. Additionally, the interconnectedness indicator now incorporates intra-financial system assets and liabilities on a gross basis, capturing contagion channels more accurately. These changes did not alter the composition of the D-SIB list but improved the methodological rigour. The framework interacts with the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) matrix: a D-SIB breaching PCA thresholds triggers accelerated supervisory action, given the systemic implications. The RBI has also signalled that as the banking sector consolidates — notably the merger of HDFC Ltd into HDFC Bank in 2023 — the systemic footprint of the combined entity will be reassessed, potentially altering bucket placement in future cycles.

RBI's Framework for Self-Regulatory Organisations in the Fintech Sector

In May 2024, the Reserve Bank of India issued the Framework for Self-Regulatory Organisations (SROs) for the FinTech Sector, formalising a co-regulatory model that delegates specific oversight functions to industry-led bodies while retaining ultimate supervisory authority. The framework responds to the rapid proliferation of fintech entities — lending platforms, payment aggregators, account aggregators, and wealth-tech providers — whose activities straddle regulatory perimeters and generate novel risks in data governance, algorithmic lending, and consumer protection.

An SRO-FT (Self-Regulatory Organisation for FinTech) must be recognised by the RBI to operate. The recognition criteria are stringent: the applicant must be a not-for-profit company (Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013) with a minimum net worth of ₹2 crore, a diversified shareholding structure (no single entity holding more than 10 per cent), and a governing board comprising independent directors, industry representatives, and nominees of the RBI. The SRO-FT must demonstrate operational capability, including a technology platform for member onboarding, compliance monitoring, and grievance redressal. Recognition is granted for an initial period of three years, renewable subject to performance review.

The mandate of an SRO-FT spans four domains. First, code of conduct: developing and enforcing standards for fair practices, transparency in pricing, data privacy, and ethical use of algorithms — particularly in credit underwriting and collection practices. Second, grievance redressal: operating a time-bound, transparent mechanism for customer complaints against members, with escalation to the RBI's Integrated Ombudsman Scheme. Third, monitoring and reporting: collecting periodic returns from members on key risk metrics (loan portfolio quality, data breaches, outsourcing risks) and submitting consolidated reports to the RBI's Department of Regulation. Fourth, capacity building: conducting training, certification, and awareness programmes for member staff and customers.

Membership in an SRO-FT is voluntary but incentivised. The RBI has indicated that SRO membership will be viewed favourably during supervisory assessments, licensing decisions (e.g., payment aggregator authorisation), and regulatory sandbox admissions. Conversely, non-members may face enhanced supervisory scrutiny. The framework also provides for disciplinary powers: an SRO-FT can impose monetary penalties (up to ₹1 crore per violation), suspend or expel members, and mandate remedial actions. Appeals against SRO decisions lie with the RBI's Executive Director in charge of regulation, ensuring regulatory oversight of the self-regulatory layer.

The first SRO-FT recognised under this framework was the FinTech Association for Consumer Empowerment (FACE), granted recognition in August 2024. FACE's founding members include major digital lending platforms, payment gateways, and account aggregators. Its initial code of conduct addresses key person risk in algorithmic models, requiring documented model governance frameworks, independent validation of credit scoring models, and a "human-in-the-loop" override for adverse decisions. The framework also anticipates the emergence of sector-specific SROs (e.g., for digital lending or wealth-tech) that could operate under an umbrella SRO-FT, creating a layered self-regulatory architecture. The RBI's 2024-25 supervisory plan explicitly includes thematic inspections of SRO-FT governance, funding independence, and the effectiveness of their disciplinary mechanisms.

Examiner's Trap: SRO-FT vs Industry Association
A question asks: "Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes a recognised SRO-FT under the RBI's 2024 framework from a conventional fintech industry association? (a) An SRO-FT can impose binding disciplinary penalties on members; an industry association cannot. (b) An SRO-FT membership is mandatory for all fintech entities; industry association membership is voluntary. (c) An SRO-FT is funded by the RBI; an industry association is member-funded. (d) An SRO-FT replaces the RBI's supervisory role; an industry association complements it."
Correct answer: (a). The framework explicitly grants recognised SRO-FTs the power to impose monetary penalties (up to ₹1 crore), suspend, or expel members for violations of the code of conduct — powers that a conventional industry association lacks. Statement (b) is incorrect because SRO-FT membership is voluntary, though incentivised. Statement (c) is incorrect: SRO-FTs must be member-funded (minimum net worth ₹2 crore) and cannot receive RBI funding. Statement (d) is incorrect: the RBI retains ultimate supervisory authority; the SRO-FT operates under RBI oversight with appeals lying to the RBI's Executive Director.
Exam-Day Strategy: Mapping Co-Regulation
When a question tests the SRO-FT framework, anchor your answer on three pillars: (1) Recognition criteria (Section 8 company, ₹2 crore net worth, diversified shareholding, RBI-nominated directors), (2) Four-function mandate (code of conduct, grievance redressal, monitoring/reporting, capacity building), and (3) Voluntary membership with regulatory incentives. Contrast this with the Payment System Operator SRO framework (2019) and the Account Aggregator SRO — each has distinct recognition paths. Memorise the first recognised SRO-FT (FACE, August 2024) and its focus on algorithmic governance. A 2-marker on "key difference from industry association" is almost certain; the binding disciplinary power is the clincher.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market: Primary Dealers, Market Making, and Credit Spread Dynamics

The transmission of monetary policy to the corporate bond market operates through distinct channels compared to the banking channel, with the credit spread — the yield differential between corporate bonds and government securities of comparable maturity — acting as the key transmission variable. The RBI's policy rate influences corporate bond yields primarily via the risk-free rate channel (changes in G-sec yields) and the risk-premium channel (changes in credit spreads driven by liquidity conditions, risk appetite, and macroeconomic outlook). Empirical studies by the RBI's Department of Economic and Policy Research indicate that the pass-through to high-rated (AAA/AA) corporate bond yields is relatively swift (60-70 per cent within two quarters), but transmission to lower-rated segments and non-bank issuers remains incomplete and asymmetric.

Primary Dealers (PDs) play a pivotal role as market makers. The RBI's Market Making Scheme for Corporate Bonds, introduced in 2018 and revised in 2021, designates PDs as obligated market makers for specified corporate bonds (initially AAA-rated public sector undertaking bonds). PDs must provide continuous two-way quotes with a maximum bid-ask spread (typically 15-25 basis points) and minimum quote size (₹5 crore). In return, they receive liquidity support — access to the RBI's repo window against corporate bond collateral (within haircut limits) and eligibility for the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) and Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) auctions. This architecture aims to compress the liquidity premium embedded in corporate bond yields, thereby improving the risk-premium channel of transmission.

The Corporate Bond Repo Facility, operationalised through the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL), allows repo transactions in corporate bonds rated AA and above. The facility uses a tri-party repo structure with CCIL as the central counterparty, mitigating counterparty risk. Haircuts are calibrated by rating bucket (e.g., 5 per cent for AAA, 10 per cent for AA) and residual maturity. This facility enables PDs and banks to fund corporate bond inventories at rates close to the policy repo rate, linking corporate bond financing costs directly to the monetary policy stance. However, utilisation remains concentrated in top-rated PSU bonds; private sector and lower-rated paper see limited repo activity due to higher haircuts and stigma risk.

Two structural factors impede fuller transmission. First, fragmented liquidity: the corporate bond market is overwhelmingly private-placement dominated (over 90 per cent of issuance), with limited secondary trading. Most bonds are held to maturity by banks, insurers, and provident funds, resulting in thin order books. Second, credit spread persistence: during tightening cycles, credit spreads widen disproportionately for lower-rated issuers as risk aversion rises, muting the pass-through of policy rate cuts during easing cycles — a phenomenon documented in the RBI's Financial Stability Reports (2022-23). The RBI has responded by permitting Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) to participate in the corporate bond repo market (2023), introducing exchange-traded corporate bond platforms (NSE/BSE request-for-quote systems), and mandating minimum public issuance (25 per cent of incremental borrowing for large corporates per SEBI's 2019 circular, though compliance timelines have been extended). The Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS) and the proposed Corporate Bond Database (centralised repository) aim to improve price discovery and transparency, which are prerequisites for efficient transmission.

Currency Management Framework: Clean Note Policy, Note Printing, and Coin Distribution Logistics

The Reserve Bank of India derives its sole currency issuance authority from Section 22 of the RBI Act, 1934. The operational management of currency — design, printing, distribution, quality maintenance, and withdrawal — is executed through a multi-layered infrastructure involving the RBI's Issue Department, two government-owned printing presses, four mints, and a network of over 4,000 currency chests and small coin depots maintained by commercial banks. The Clean Note Policy, first articulated in 1999 and comprehensively revised in 2018, sets the standards for note quality, public exchange facilities, and the withdrawal of soiled and mutilated notes.

Note printing is undertaken at four presses: two owned by the Security Printing and Minting Corporation of India Ltd (SPMCIL) at Nashik (Maharashtra) and Dewas (Madhya Pradesh), and two by the Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Pvt Ltd (BRBNMPL) — a wholly owned RBI subsidiary — at Mysuru (Karnataka) and Salboni (West Bengal). The annual indent is placed by the RBI based on demand projections (using the currency-to-GDP ratio, seasonal patterns, and replacement rates). In FY 2023-24, the combined production capacity exceeded 16 billion pieces. The Mahatma Gandhi (New) Series, introduced from 2016 onwards, incorporates enhanced security features: see-through register, latent image, micro-lettering, colour-shifting ink (₹500 and ₹2,000), and angular bleed lines for the visually impaired. The ₹2,000 denomination was withdrawn from circulation in May 2023 (though it remains legal tender) to align with the Clean Note Policy's objective of reducing high-denomination stock.

Coin minting is the exclusive domain of SPMCIL at four mints: Mumbai, Hyderabad, Kolkata, and Noida. Coins are issued in denominations of 50 paise, ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10, and ₹20. The ₹20 coin (dodecagonal, bi-metallic) was introduced in 2019. The RBI distributes coins through its regional offices to currency chests, which then supply bank branches. A persistent challenge is the coin recirculation gap: coins accumulate in temples, households, and the informal sector, leading to periodic shortages despite adequate minting. The RBI has launched coin exchange melas and mandated banks to accept coins in any quantity (though practical limits apply at counters).

The currency chest system is the backbone of distribution. As of March 2024, there were 3,054 currency chests (held by public sector, private sector, and foreign banks) and 3,748 small coin depots. Chests are reimbursed for chest-to-chest remittances and chest-to-branch movements. The RBI monitors chest balances through the Currency Management System (CMS), a real-time dashboard tracking denomination-wise stocks, indent status, and soiled note receipts. The Note Sorting Machines (NSMs) — mandated at all currency chests and high-volume branches — authenticate, sort, and destroy soiled notes. Notes deemed unfit are shredded and briquetted; the briquettes are tendered for industrial use (e.g., cement kilns). The 2018 Clean Note Policy revision introduced time-bound exchange commitments: banks must exchange soiled/mutilated notes up to ₹5,000 per day per person over the counter without form-filling; higher amounts require documentation. The policy also prohibits stapling of note packets (to prevent damage) and mandates the use of banded packets with paper bands.

Recent innovations include the star series notes (replacement notes with a * in the number panel) for defective prints detected during quality control, and the varnished ₹100 notes (pilot 2023) to extend circulation life. The RBI's Annual Report 2023-24 notes that the volume of banknotes in circulation reached ₹34.4 lakh crore (12.1 per cent of GDP), with ₹500 notes constituting 48 per cent of value and ₹10 notes leading in volume share. The cost of currency management (printing, distribution, destruction) was ₹4,900 crore in FY 2023-24, down from ₹5,800 crore in the demonetisation year (FY 2016-17), reflecting economies of scale and improved note life.

RBI's Integrated Ombudsman Scheme: Architecture, Jurisdiction, and Emerging Jurisprudence

Launched in November 2021, the Reserve Bank — Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS), 2021 unified three pre-existing ombudsman schemes — Banking Ombudsman Scheme (2006), Ombudsman Scheme for Non-Banking Financial Companies (2018), and Ombudsman Scheme for Digital Transactions (2019) — into a single, jurisdiction-neutral framework. The integration eliminated regulatory arbitrage where a customer's grievance could fall between cracks (e.g., a digital transaction initiated through a bank's app but processed by an NBFC payment aggregator). The Scheme operates under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, Section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934, and Section 18 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.

The institutional architecture comprises a Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre (CRPC) at Chandigarh, which handles intake, language translation, and initial scrutiny of all complaints received via the Complaint Management System (CMS) portal, email, or physical post. Complaints are then assigned to one of the 22 Offices of the Ombudsman (located in state capitals and major cities) based on the regulated entity's registered office or the complainant's residence. Each Office is headed by an Ombudsman (appointed by the RBI for a three-year term, extendable by two years) supported by a legal and technical staff. The Appellate Authority is the Executive Director-in-charge of the Consumer Education and Protection Department (CEPD) at the RBI Central Office, Mumbai — a critical design feature ensuring that appeals remain within the RBI's supervisory chain rather than migrating to external tribunals.

Jurisdiction covers "deficiency in service" as defined in the Scheme: failure to adhere to RBI directions, unfair practices, non-observance of fair practices codes, levying charges without prior notice, and delays in service. The Scheme explicitly includes credit card, debit card, and prepaid payment instrument grievances; loan servicing issues (recovery agent harassment, incorrect interest charging); digital payment failures (UPI, IMPS, wallet transactions); and NBFC-specific complaints (gold loan auction irregularities, microfinance coercive recovery). The pecuniary jurisdiction allows compensation up to ₹20 lakh for actual financial loss and up to ₹1 lakh for mental agony and harassment. The Ombudsman can also direct non-monetary remedies: rectification of credit information, issuance of no-dues certificates, and cessation of unfair practices.

The process timeline is strictly defined: the regulated entity (RE) must respond within 21 days of the complaint being forwarded; the Ombudsman endeavours to pass an award within 90 days of receipt (extendable by 30 days in complex cases). The RE can appeal within 30 days; the Appellate Authority decides within 45 days. The Scheme incorporates a precedent value mechanism: awards involving novel interpretations are published (anonymised) on the RBI website, guiding future decisions. The Annual Report of the Ombudsman Schemes (2023-24) reveals that 7.2 lakh complaints were received, a 68 per cent year-on-year increase, driven by digital payment grievances (42 per cent share) and credit card disputes (18 per cent). The disposal rate was 94 per cent, with 61 per cent of maintainable complaints resolved in favour of the complainant. The top three grounds were: non-observance of RBI directions on credit card conduct (2022 master direction), UPI transaction failures beyond T+1 reversal timelines, and levy of foreclosure charges on floating-rate loans in violation of the 2012 circular.

Recent jurisprudential developments include: (1) vicarious liability of banks for recovery agent misconduct — the Ombudsman has held banks liable for harassment by outsourced agents, directing compensation and blacklisting of agencies; (2) algorithmic accountability — in a 2023 award, an NBFC was directed to disclose the key variables of its credit scoring model to a rejected applicant, establishing a transparency precedent; (3) shared liability in failed UPI transactions — where the failure originated at the payer bank but the beneficiary bank delayed reversal, both were directed to share compensation. The RBI's 2024 Review of the RB-IOS proposed expanding the Scheme to cover regulated entities under the Factoring Regulation Act and account aggregators, and introducing a video-hearing facility for complainants in remote areas.

  • Confusing the D-SIB surcharge with the G-SIB surcharge; India has no G-SIBs (global systemically important banks), and the D-SIB surcharge is domestic-only, calibrated to buckets 1-5 (0.20%-1.00% CET1).
  • Assuming SRO-FT membership is mandatory for fintech licensing; it is voluntary but carries supervisory incentives — the RBI has not made it a licensing condition for payment aggregators or account aggregators.
  • Believing corporate bond repo is available for all ratings; the CCIL facility is restricted to AA and above, with haircuts rising sharply below AAA — below-investment-grade bonds are ineligible.
  • Thinking the Clean Note Policy permits stapling note packets; the 2018 revision explicitly prohibits stapling and mandates paper bands to prevent note damage.
  • Assuming the Integrated Ombudsman can adjudicate interest rate disputes on fixed-rate loans; the Scheme covers "deficiency in service" but not commercial judgment on contracted rates unless the rate violates an RBI circular (e.g., floating-rate foreclosure charges).
  • Overlooking that the D-SIB assessment uses leverage ratio exposure, not total assets; the 2022 methodology shift improved cross-border comparability but did not change the list.
  • Confusing the Appellate Authority under RB-IOS with the Banking Ombudsman's pre-2021 appellate mechanism; appeals now lie with the RBI's Executive Director (CEPD), not a separate tribunal.

Digital Rupee Retail Pilot: Architecture, Use Cases, and Policy Implications

The Reserve Bank of India launched the retail Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC‑R) pilot on 1 December 2022 in four cities — Mumbai, New Delhi, Bengaluru and Bhubaneswar — with eight participating banks: State Bank of India, ICICI Bank, Yes Bank, IDFC First Bank, Bank of Baroda, Union Bank of India, HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank. The pilot uses a token‑based, account‑less model where each digital rupee unit is a cryptographically signed token issued by the RBI and held in a user’s digital wallet on a smartphone. Transactions are settled instantly on a permissioned distributed ledger operated by the RBI, providing finality without the need for inter‑bank clearing. The architecture separates the issuance layer (RBI), the distribution layer (banks) and the user layer (wallet apps), allowing banks to onboard customers, perform KYC and manage wallet lifecycle while the RBI retains sole authority over token creation and redemption.

Key use cases tested include person‑to‑person (P2P) payments, person‑to‑merchant (P2M) QR‑code payments, offline proximity payments using Near‑Field Communication (NFC) and programmable money features such as purpose‑bound vouchers for fertiliser subsidies. The pilot also evaluates interoperability with existing payment rails: UPI QR codes can be used to accept CBDC‑R, and users can convert bank deposits into digital rupee and vice‑versa at par. Early data from the RBI’s 2023‑24 Annual Report shows daily transaction volumes rising from a few thousand in January 2023 to over 1.2 million by March 2024, with merchant acceptance points exceeding 2.5 lakh. The pilot’s offline capability was demonstrated in a controlled environment where two wallets exchanged tokens via Bluetooth without internet connectivity, addressing financial inclusion in low‑connectivity regions.

Policy implications are significant. First, CBDC‑R provides the central bank with a direct monetary policy transmission channel — interest‑bearing CBDC could allow negative rates to be passed to households. Second, it reduces settlement risk and the cost of currency management; the RBI estimates a potential saving of ₹4,000 crore annually on printing, distribution and replacement of physical notes. Third, the programmable nature enables targeted fiscal transfers, reducing leakage in subsidy programmes. However, challenges remain: disintermediation risk if households shift large deposits to CBDC‑R, necessitating a calibrated holding limit (currently ₹2 lakh per wallet); privacy concerns, as the RBI can trace every token movement; and the need for robust cyber‑resilience given the single ledger architecture. The RBI’s 2024 consultation paper on CBDC‑R design seeks feedback on holding limits, interest‑bearing features, and a phased nationwide rollout by 2026.

RBI's Cybersecurity and IT Governance Framework for Banks and NBFCs

The RBI’s cybersecurity framework has evolved through three major milestones. The 2011 “Guidelines on Information Security, Electronic Banking, Technology Risk Management and Cyber Frauds” mandated a board‑approved information security policy, a dedicated Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) and periodic vulnerability assessments. In June 2016, the RBI issued a comprehensive “Cyber Security Framework in Banks” circular requiring banks to adopt a baseline set of controls aligned with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, establish a Security Operations Centre (SOC) with 24×7 monitoring, and report cyber incidents within two to six hours depending on severity. The 2021 “Master Direction – Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices” extended these requirements to all scheduled commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks and NBFCs with asset size above ₹5,000 crore, prescribing a governance structure with a Board‑level IT Strategy Committee, an IT Steering Committee and an independent audit of IT controls.

The 2023 “Cyber Security Framework for Banks – Revised” introduced a risk‑based approach: banks must classify themselves into four tiers based on systemic importance, digital footprint and threat exposure. Tier 1 (D‑SIBs and large universal banks) are required to implement advanced threat intelligence sharing, red‑team exercises quarterly, and a dedicated Cyber Crisis Management Plan tested annually. Tier 2 and 3 banks follow a proportionate set of controls, while Tier 4 (small NBFCs, regional rural banks) adopt a simplified baseline. The framework also mandates encryption of data at rest and in transit, multi‑factor authentication for all privileged access, and a minimum 180‑day log retention. Non‑compliance attracts supervisory action under the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) matrix, including restrictions on new digital product launches.

For NBFCs, the 2022 “Guidelines on Information Technology Framework for NBFCs” aligned their obligations with banks, requiring a CISO, a board‑approved IT policy, and quarterly reporting of cyber incidents to the RBI’s Department of Supervision. The RBI’s 2024 “Cyber Resilience Index” pilot, covering 30 large banks, scores institutions on governance, detection, response and recovery capabilities; results feed into the supervisory rating. A notable enforcement case occurred in 2023 when a major private sector bank was fined ₹2 crore for delayed reporting of a ransomware attack that compromised customer data, underscoring the RBI’s zero‑tolerance stance on incident disclosure.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which of the following is NOT a mandatory requirement under the RBI’s 2023 revised Cyber Security Framework for Tier 1 banks?” Options: (a) Quarterly red‑team exercises, (b) Annual Cyber Crisis Management Plan test, (c) Real‑time threat intelligence sharing with the RBI, (d) Mandatory adoption of ISO 27001 certification.
The correct answer is (d). The 2023 framework prescribes quarterly red‑team exercises, annual crisis‑plan testing, and participation in the RBI‑facilitated threat‑intelligence sharing platform, but it does not make ISO 27001 certification mandatory; banks may adopt any equivalent standard. This trap tests whether the aspirant confuses recommended best practice with regulatory mandate.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question cites a specific RBI circular year, map it to the corresponding framework tier. Remember: 2011 = baseline, 2016 = NIST‑aligned controls, 2021 = governance extension to NBFCs, 2023 = tiered risk‑based approach. A quick mental timeline prevents mixing up requirements across versions.

RBI's Outsourcing and Cloud Services Guidelines for Regulated Entities

The RBI first addressed outsourcing risk in a 2017 circular “Outsourcing of Financial Services by Banks”, which required banks to retain ultimate responsibility for outsourced activities, conduct due‑diligence on service providers, and include audit‑right clauses in contracts. The 2021 “Master Direction – Outsourcing of IT Services by Banks, NBFCs and Other Regulated Entities” consolidated and expanded these norms. It defines “material outsourcing” as any arrangement where the failure of the service provider could materially impact the regulated entity’s (RE’s) operations, reputation or regulatory compliance. REs must maintain a register of all material outsourcing arrangements, obtain prior approval from the Board’s Risk Management Committee for new material contracts, and ensure the service provider’s data centres are located in India unless the RBI grants a specific exemption.

Cloud adoption received dedicated guidance in the 2022 “Guidelines on Adoption of Cloud Services by Regulated Entities”. The guidelines classify cloud deployment models — public, private, community and hybrid — and require REs to adopt a “cloud‑first” strategy only after a comprehensive risk assessment covering data sovereignty, vendor lock‑in, concentration risk and exit strategy. Critical data (customer PII, transaction logs, encryption keys) must reside in India‑based data centres. REs must negotiate contractual “right to audit” and “right to data portability” clauses, and conduct annual third‑party penetration testing of the cloud environment. The RBI also mandated that REs maintain a “cloud exit plan” tested at least once every two years, ensuring business continuity if the cloud provider fails or the contract terminates.

Supervisory oversight is exercised through the RBI’s “IT Examination” framework, where examiners verify the outsourcing register, review service‑level agreements (SLAs) for availability (≥99.9 % for critical systems), incident‑response coordination, and the RE’s ability to monitor the provider’s sub‑contractors. In 2023, the RBI issued a supervisory letter to a large NBFC for inadequate oversight of a third‑party KYC verification vendor, resulting in a ₹50 lakh penalty and a directive to bring the function in‑house within six months. The evolving framework reflects the RBI’s intent to balance fintech‑driven innovation with the systemic imperative of operational resilience.

Cross-Border UPI Linkages: Singapore PayNow, UAE UPI, and the Roadmap for Rupee Internationalisation

India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) became the first real‑time payment system to achieve live cross‑border interoperability when the UPI‑PayNow linkage with Singapore went live on 21 February 2023. The arrangement allows users of participating banks in India (initially State Bank of India, Indian Overseas Bank, Indian Bank and ICICI Bank) and Singapore (DBS/POSB, OCBC, UOB and Standard Chartered) to send and receive funds instantly using only a mobile number or Virtual Payment Address (VPA). The technical integration uses the NPCI‑developed “UPI‑Link” protocol, which maps UPI identifiers to PayNow proxies and settles transactions in real time through a bilateral settlement account maintained at the RBI and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS). Transaction limits are set at SGD 1,000 (≈ ₹60,000) per transaction and SGD 5,000 per day, with zero merchant discount rate for P2P flows.

A second corridor, UPI‑UAE, was launched on 12 July 2023 in partnership with the Central Bank of the UAE and the payment operator “UAE Payments”. It enables Indian tourists and the large diaspora to make QR‑code payments at UAE merchants using their home UPI apps, while UAE residents can pay Indian merchants via the “Bharat Interface for Money” (BHIM) app. Settlement occurs in Indian rupees through a vostro account held by a UAE bank at the RBI, eliminating the need for dollar intermediation. The RBI’s 2024 “Vision Document on Cross‑Border Payments” outlines a phased roadmap: (1) expand UPI linkages to at least ten jurisdictions by 2026, prioritising high‑remittance corridors such as the USA, UK, Saudi Arabia and Malaysia; (2) enable rupee‑denominated settlement for trade invoices via the “Rupee Vostro” mechanism, already operational with 18 partner banks across 12 countries; (3) integrate UPI with the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub’s “Project Nexus” to achieve multilateral interoperability.

Policy benefits include reduced remittance costs (World Bank estimates a 2‑3 % saving versus traditional SWIFT channels), faster settlement (seconds versus T+1), and enhanced rupee internationalisation by creating natural demand for rupee liquidity abroad. Risks involve AML/CFT compliance across jurisdictions, operational dependency on foreign central bank infrastructures, and the need for harmonised dispute‑resolution frameworks. The RBI has mandated that all cross‑border UPI transactions undergo real‑time screening against the UN sanctions list and that participating banks report suspicious patterns to the Financial Intelligence Unit‑India (FIU‑IND) within 24 hours.

  • Confusing the CBDC‑R holding limit (₹2 lakh) with the UPI daily transaction limit (₹1 lakh for most banks).
  • Assuming the 2023 Cyber Security Framework makes ISO 27001 certification mandatory for Tier 1 banks.
  • Believing cloud data residency rules allow critical data to be stored in any “trusted” foreign data centre without RBI exemption.
  • Thinking the UPI‑PayNow linkage settles in US dollars; it settles in SGD/INR via bilateral accounts.
  • Overlooking that the RBI’s outsourcing master direction applies to NBFCs above ₹5,000 crore, not all NBFCs.
  • Mixing up the “right to audit” clause in cloud contracts with a general right to inspect the vendor’s premises without notice.
  • Assuming the Rupee Vostro mechanism is available for all current‑account transactions; it is currently limited to trade‑related payments.

The advanced sections above deepen understanding of emerging RBI frameworks that frequently appear in analytical questions.

RBI’s Co‑Lending Framework and Priority Sector Lending Integration

The Reserve Bank of India introduced the co‑lending model through a circular dated 5 November 2020, allowing scheduled commercial banks and eligible non‑banking financial companies (NBFCs) to jointly extend credit to priority sector borrowers. The framework mandates a minimum 80:20 risk‑sharing ratio, with the bank retaining at least 80 per cent of the credit risk on its balance sheet and the NBFC holding the remaining 20 per cent. Both parties must conduct independent credit appraisal, but the final sanction rests with the bank. The model is applicable to all priority sector categories — agriculture, micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), export credit, education, housing, social infrastructure, renewable energy and others — provided the borrower meets the sector‑specific eligibility criteria.

Operationally, the bank and NBFC enter into a master agreement that defines the origination, underwriting, documentation, monitoring and recovery responsibilities. The NBFC typically originates the loan, leveraging its niche distribution network, while the bank provides the bulk of the funding and ensures compliance with prudential norms such as the Large Exposure Framework and the Capital Adequacy Requirements. The RBI requires that the co‑lending portfolio be reported separately in the bank’s quarterly returns, and that the NBFC’s exposure be captured in its own regulatory returns. Since inception, the co‑lending book has grown steadily; as of March 2024, banks reported co‑lending outstanding of approximately ₹1.2 lakh crore, with MSMEs accounting for roughly 55 per cent of the volume.

The integration with priority sector lending (PSL) targets has been a key driver. Banks can count the entire co‑lending exposure toward their PSL sub‑targets, while the NBFC’s share does not dilute the bank’s PSL achievement. This feature has encouraged banks to partner with NBFCs that have strong last‑mile reach in rural and semi‑urban areas. However, the framework also imposes safeguards: the NBFC must maintain a minimum net owned fund of ₹25 crore, a capital adequacy ratio of 15 per cent, and a track record of at least three years in the relevant lending segment. The RBI’s 2023 review highlighted concerns around concentration risk — some banks had over 30 per cent of their co‑lending book tied to a single NBFC — prompting a directive to diversify counterparties.

From a transmission perspective, co‑lending improves monetary policy pass‑through to underserved segments because the bank’s marginal cost of funds influences the pricing of the entire loan. The NBFC’s higher cost of funds is limited to its 20 per cent share, reducing the overall lending rate. Empirical studies by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) suggest that co‑lending loans to MSMEs are priced 30‑50 basis points lower than comparable standalone NBFC loans. The model also supports financial inclusion by extending formal credit to borrowers who lack collateral but have cash‑flow based repayment capacity, a segment traditionally served by informal lenders.

Digital Lending Guidelines 2022: First Loss Default Guarantee, Algorithmic Credit Scoring, and Consumer Protection

In September 2022 the RBI issued comprehensive guidelines for digital lending, applicable to all regulated entities (REs) — banks, NBFCs, and payment system operators — that originate loans through digital platforms, including those operated by third‑party fintech firms. The guidelines address three pillars: the First Loss Default Guarantee (FLDG), algorithmic credit scoring transparency, and consumer protection measures.

The FLDG provision permits REs to offer a guarantee covering the first loss on a digital loan portfolio, capped at 5 per cent of the outstanding portfolio or ₹5 crore, whichever is lower. The guarantee must be backed by the RE’s own capital, not by the fintech partner, and must be disclosed in the loan agreement. This cap prevents the guarantee from becoming a de‑facto credit enhancement that circumvents capital adequacy rules. The RBI also requires that the FLDG be accounted for as a contingent liability and that the RE maintain a minimum capital charge of 100 per cent on the guaranteed portion.

On algorithmic credit scoring, the guidelines mandate that any model used for credit decisions be documented, validated, and auditable. REs must maintain a model inventory, conduct annual independent validation, and ensure that the model does not use prohibited variables such as caste, religion, or gender. The output of the model — score, risk grade, and key drivers — must be communicated to the borrower in plain language at the time of sanction. The RBI’s 2023 supervisory letter to a large NBFC highlighted a case where an opaque machine‑learning model led to systematic exclusion of borrowers from certain geographic pin‑codes, resulting in a penalty of ₹1 crore and a directive to rebuild the model with explainability constraints.

Consumer protection provisions include a mandatory key facts statement (KFS) delivered electronically before loan execution, a cooling‑off period of 24 hours for loans up to ₹5 lakh, and a grievance redressal mechanism with a maximum turnaround of 30 days. REs must also ensure that digital lending apps do not access contacts, location, or camera data beyond what is necessary for KYC. The guidelines prohibit automatic renewal of loans without explicit borrower consent and require that all fees, including processing charges and penal interest, be disclosed upfront. Early data from the RBI’s Digital Lending Monitoring Cell indicates that compliance has reduced the average number of borrower complaints per 1,000 digital loans from 12 in Q3 2022 to 4 in Q4 2023.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Under the RBI’s 2022 Digital Lending Guidelines, what is the maximum permissible First Loss Default Guarantee (FLDG) as a percentage of the outstanding digital loan portfolio?” Options: (a) 2 per cent, (b) 5 per cent, (c) 10 per cent, (d) No limit.
The correct answer is (b) 5 per cent. The guidelines explicitly cap the FLDG at 5 per cent of the outstanding portfolio or ₹5 crore, whichever is lower. This limit ensures that the guarantee does not become a substitute for adequate capital and remains a contingent liability subject to a 100 per cent capital charge. Candidates often confuse this with the 2 per cent limit applicable to credit guarantees under the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE), which is a separate scheme.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question cites a specific RBI circular (e.g., “September 2022 Digital Lending Guidelines”), locate the key numerical caps — FLDG 5 per cent, cooling‑off 24 hours, grievance redressal 30 days — and match them to the options. Remember that the FLDG cap is on the portfolio, not on individual loans, and that the guarantee must be backed by the RE’s own capital. This distinction eliminates distractors referencing fintech‑backed guarantees.

RBI’s Cyber Resilience and Cloud Outsourcing Framework for Regulated Entities

The RBI’s cyber resilience framework rests on two principal instruments: the “Cyber Security Framework for Banks” issued in June 2021 and the “Master Direction on Outsourcing of Information Technology Services” released in April 2023. Together they prescribe a layered defence for all REs — commercial banks, NBFCs above ₹5,000 crore asset size, payment system operators, and authorised payment system participants.

The 2021 framework mandates a board‑approved cyber security policy, a dedicated Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), and a Security Operations Centre (SOC) capable of 24 × 7 monitoring. REs must conduct a comprehensive vulnerability assessment at least annually and a penetration test semi‑annually. Incident reporting is time‑bound: any material cyber incident must be reported to the RBI within six hours of detection, followed by a detailed root‑cause analysis within 30 days. The framework also requires REs to maintain a cyber insurance cover commensurate with their risk profile, with a minimum sum insured of ₹10 crore for banks and ₹5 crore for NBFCs.

The 2023 outsourcing master direction extends these requirements to cloud service providers (CSPs). REs may only engage CSPs that meet the RBI’s “cloud eligibility criteria”, which include data residency in India for critical systems, ISO 27001 certification, and a contractual “right to audit” clause allowing the RE and the RBI to inspect the CSP’s infrastructure, logs, and sub‑contractor arrangements. The direction mandates a cloud exit plan tested at least once every two years, ensuring business continuity if the CSP fails or the contract terminates. SLAs for critical systems must guarantee availability of ≥99.9 per cent, with penalties for breaches. In 2023 the RBI imposed a ₹50 lakh penalty on a large NBFC for inadequate oversight of a third‑party KYC verification vendor, directing the NBFC to bring the function in‑house within six months.

Supervisory oversight is exercised through the RBI’s IT Examination framework, where examiners verify the outsourcing register, review SLAs, assess incident‑response coordination, and evaluate the RE’s ability to monitor the CSP’s sub‑contractors. The evolving framework reflects the RBI’s intent to balance fintech‑driven innovation with the systemic imperative of operational resilience. REs that fail to comply face graduated enforcement actions ranging from supervisory letters to monetary penalties and, in extreme cases, restriction on new digital product launches.

Retail CBDC Pilot: Architecture, Distribution Model, and Early Transaction Data

The Reserve Bank launched the retail Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC‑R) pilot on 1 December 2022, initially covering four cities — Mumbai, New Delhi, Bengaluru, and Bhubaneswar — and eight participating banks. The CBDC‑R is a token‑based, legal tender issued directly by the RBI, designed to complement cash rather than replace it. Unlike the wholesale CBDC (CBDC‑W) which uses a centralised ledger for interbank settlement, the retail variant employs a distributed ledger technology (DLT) platform built on a permissioned blockchain, allowing peer‑to‑peer transfers without an intermediary.

The distribution follows a two‑tier model: the RBI issues CBDC‑R to the participating banks (Tier 1), which in turn distribute it to end‑users through their existing mobile banking applications (Tier 2). Users hold CBDC‑R in a digital wallet that stores cryptographic keys; transactions are authorised by the wallet app and settled instantly on the DLT network. The pilot supports both online and offline modes — offline transactions use near‑field communication (NFC) and are limited to ₹2,000 per transaction and ₹10,000 per day per wallet, with subsequent synchronisation when connectivity is restored.

As of March 2024, the pilot had onboarded approximately 1.2 million users and processed over 3.5 million transactions, with a cumulative volume of ₹1,200 crore. The average transaction size was ₹340, indicating predominant use for low‑value retail payments such as grocery purchases, utility bills, and peer‑to‑peer transfers. The RBI’s interim report highlighted that 68 per cent of transactions occurred in online mode, while offline usage was concentrated in areas with intermittent connectivity. The pilot also tested interoperability with the Unified Payments Interface (UPI); users could convert CBDC‑R to UPI balances and vice‑versa through participating bank apps, with settlement finality achieved within seconds.

Key design choices include a holding limit of ₹2 lakh per wallet to mitigate disintermediation risk, and a non‑interest‑bearing nature to preserve the monetary policy transmission channel. The RBI has stated that the pilot will be expanded to additional cities and banks in a phased manner, with a focus on evaluating the impact on currency demand, financial inclusion, and the resilience of the payment ecosystem. Lessons from the pilot are expected to inform the final design of a full‑scale retail CBDC, including potential integration with the Account Aggregator framework for consent‑based data sharing.
