hand/derived-algebraic-geometry.html:
Higher Stacks and ∞‑Topoi in Derived Geometry

The passage from derived schemes to higher stacks is forced by the need to represent moduli functors not representable by derived schemes alone. An ∞‑topos is an ∞‑category of sheaves of spaces on a Grothendieck site satisfying descent for hypercovers. In derived algebraic geometry the étale site of a simplicial commutative ring (or an E∞‑ring spectrum) carries a structure sheaf valued in connective E∞‑ring spectra; the resulting ∞‑topos of sheaves of spaces is the ambient ∞‑category for derived stacks. Lurie’s representability theorem in Higher Algebra gives necessary and sufficient conditions for a functor F : CAlg^cn → Spaces to be a derived stack: (i) F preserves limits, (ii) F satisfies étale hyperdescent, and (iii) the relative cotangent complex LF/S is connective and of finite presentation. These conditions are the derived analogue of Artin’s criteria for algebraic stacks. The ∞‑topos formalism also supplies a robust geometric realization: any simplicial object has a colimit, used to construct quotient stacks such as [X/G] for a derived group scheme G acting on a derived scheme X. Hyperdescent guarantees the quotient is a derived stack, and its cotangent complex fits into a fiber sequence L[X/G]/S → LX/S → 𝔤^* ⊗ O_X[1] where 𝔤 is the Lie algebra of G. This sequence is the derived version of the exact sequence of Kähler differentials for a quotient by a smooth group action. The ∞‑topos perspective clarifies the relation to classical stacks: the truncation functor τ≤0 from the ∞‑topos of derived stacks to the ordinary 2‑topos of Artin stacks is left exact and preserves finite limits, so classical moduli problems embed fully faithfully. In practice one works with a model such as the Joyal–Jardine model structure on simplicial presheaves or the complete Segal space model; both give equivalent homotopy theories and allow concrete computation of mapping spaces via derived Hom complexes.

Derived Intersection Theory and Virtual Pullbacks

Classical intersection theory fails when cycles meet in the wrong dimension or with excess intersection. Derived algebraic geometry replaces the ordinary fiber product X ×_Z Y by the derived fiber product X ×^R_Z Y, the homotopy pullback in the ∞‑category of derived schemes. The structure sheaf of the derived fiber product is the derived tensor product O_X ⊗^LO_Z O_Y, whose homotopy groups are Tor_iO_Z(O_X, O_Y). When the maps are Tor‑independent (all higher Tor vanish), the derived fiber product coincides with the classical one and the intersection is regular. In the non‑Tor‑independent case the derived fiber product carries a perfect obstruction theory given by the relative cotangent complex LX×^R_Z Y / X×Y. The virtual fundamental class [X×^R_Z Y]vir is defined as the Gysin pullback of the fundamental class of the ambient derived scheme along the zero section of the obstruction theory. Concretely, if i : X → Z and j : Y → Z are regular embeddings of codimensions c and d, the virtual dimension of the derived intersection is dim X + dim Y − dim Z. The virtual class lives in the Chow group Avir(X×^R_Z Y) and satisfies the expected functorialities: proper pushforward, flat pullback, and the excess intersection formula becomes a statement about the Euler class of the excess normal bundle, now a perfect complex. The derived Gysin map i^! : A_*(Z) → A*-c(X) is constructed by pulling back to the derived fiber product X ×^R_Z Z ≃ X and then applying the virtual fundamental class. This formalism recovers the Fulton–MacPherson intersection product and extends it to arbitrary morphisms of derived schemes. In enumerative geometry, the virtual class of the derived moduli of stable maps to a target variety X is precisely the class used in Gromov–Witten theory; the derived language makes the construction of the obstruction theory canonical and functorial.

Worked Example: Virtual Dimension of a Derived Intersection
Let Z = A4 = Spec k[x,y,u,v]. Let X = V(x,y) and Y = V(x,u) be two planes in Z, both regularly embedded of codimension 2. Compute the virtual dimension of the derived intersection X ×^R_Z Y.
The classical intersection is W = X ∩ Y = V(x,y,u), a line (dimension 1). The expected dimension is dim X + dim Y − dim Z = 2+2−4 = 0, so the intersection is in excess by 1. The derived fiber product has structure sheaf O_X ⊗^LO_Z O_Y. Since both embeddings are regular, the Tor groups are the homology of the Koszul complex. One finds Tor0 = O_W and Tor1 = O_W (the excess normal bundle), with Tor_i = 0 for i ≥ 2. The obstruction theory is the perfect complex [O_W → O_W] concentrated in degrees 0 and −1, of virtual rank 0. The virtual dimension is the expected dimension 0. The virtual fundamental class is the Euler class of the obstruction theory, which equals the fundamental class of the line W pushed forward to the derived intersection.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a virtual dimension, first compute the expected dimension using classical codimensions, then check whether the maps are Tor‑independent. If they are not, identify the non‑vanishing Tor groups; each Tor_i in degree i contributes an obstruction space of rank equal to its length. The virtual dimension is the expected dimension minus the alternating sum of ranks of the obstruction spaces. Practice this on simple complete intersections and on the self‑intersection of a divisor with normal crossings.

Shifted Poisson Structures and Quantization

The Pantev–Toën–Vezzosi–Benkhalifa (PTVV) theory of shifted symplectic structures has a Poisson counterpart: a k‑shifted Poisson structure on a derived stack X is a map of Lie algebras Sym(T_X[−k]) → O_X satisfying the Leibniz rule, equivalently a bivector field π ∈ Γ(X, ∧2 T_X[k]) with [π,π]=0 in the shifted Schouten bracket. When k=0 this recovers ordinary Poisson structures; k=1 gives the derived critical locus of a function, where the Poisson bracket is the derived version of the canonical symplectic form on the cotangent bundle; k=−1 yields a shifted Poisson structure corresponding to a 0‑shifted symplectic structure after a degree shift. The quantization problem asks for a deformation of the structure sheaf O_X to a sheaf of Ek+1‑algebras (or E2‑algebras for k=0) whose classical limit recovers the given Poisson bracket. In derived geometry, the existence of a quantization is controlled by the cohomology of the shifted Poisson complex; the obstruction lies in H2(X, O_X) for k=0 and in higher cohomology groups for other shifts. For derived critical loci of a function f on a smooth scheme, the 1‑shifted symplectic structure is exact, and the quantization is given by the derived algebra of functions on the critical locus equipped with the star product coming from the Batalin–Vilkovisky formalism. In the context of the derived moduli of local systems on a curve, the (−1)‑shifted symplectic structure on the character stack yields a 0‑shifted Poisson structure after applying the derived loop space functor; its quantization is expected to produce the category of D‑modules on the moduli of bundles, realizing the geometric Langlands correspondence. The shifted Poisson formalism also underlies the AKSZ construction of topological field theories: a (−1)‑shifted symplectic derived stack gives a classical BV theory, and its quantization produces a factorization algebra on the source manifold.

Derived Deformation Theory of Algebras and Hochschild Cohomology

The derived deformation theory of an associative algebra A over a field k is governed by its Hochschild cochain complex C^*(A,A) equipped with the Gerstenhaber bracket. In the language of derived algebraic geometry, the moduli functor Def_A : CAlg^cn_k → Spaces sending a connective cdga R to the space of A_∞‑algebra structures on A ⊗^L_k R lifting the given structure on A is represented by a formal derived stack whose tangent complex at the base point is C^*(A,A)[1]. The Maurer–Cartan equation in the dg Lie algebra C^*(A,A)[1] encodes infinitesimal deformations, and the higher homotopies of the A_∞‑structure correspond to higher obstructions living in HHi+2(A,A). The derived Morita theorem (Toën) states that the ∞‑category of modules over a derived algebra A is equivalent to the ∞‑category of modules over any derived algebra B that is derived Morita equivalent to A; consequently, the Hochschild cohomology HH^*(A,A) is an invariant of the derived Morita equivalence class. This invariance is crucial for the derived categorical approach to mirror symmetry, where the Fukaya category of a symplectic manifold is expected to be derived Morita equivalent to the derived category of coherent sheaves on the mirror. The derived deformation functor of a dg category C is represented by the formal derived stack associated to the Hochschild cochain complex of C; its tangent complex is HH^*(C,C)[1]. The formality of the Hochschild cochain complex (Kontsevich’s formality theorem) implies that the deformation theory of a smooth algebraic variety is unobstructed and governed by polyvector fields. In the derived setting, the formality extends to derived stacks with a shifted symplectic structure, giving a canonical quantization of the shifted Poisson bracket via the Ek+1‑operad.

Applications to Mirror Symmetry and Fukaya Categories

Homological mirror symmetry (HMS) predicts an equivalence between the derived Fukaya category Fuk(M) of a Calabi–Yau symplectic manifold M and the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves D^b Coh(M^∨) on the mirror complex manifold M^∨. Derived algebraic geometry provides the natural framework to formulate and prove such equivalences. The Fukaya category is an A_∞‑category whose objects are Lagrangian submanifolds equipped with local systems; its derived version is obtained by taking the derived category of right modules over the A_∞‑category. On the B‑side, the derived category of coherent sheaves is the derived category of a derived scheme (or derived stack) that encodes the complex structure of M^∨. The closed‑open string map identifies the Hochschild cohomology of Fuk(M) with the quantum cohomology of M, while on the B‑side it identifies HH^*(D^b Coh(M^∨)) with the polyvector fields on M^∨. The derived deformation theory of both sides is controlled by the same shifted Poisson structure: the symplectic form on M gives a 0‑shifted symplectic structure on the derived moduli of objects in Fuk(M), and the holomorphic volume form on M^∨ gives a (−1)‑shifted symplectic structure on the derived moduli of objects in D^b Coh(M^∨). PTVV established the equivalence of these shifted symplectic structures for certain toric Calabi–Yau varieties. Moreover, the derived category of singularities of a Landau–Ginzburg model (the derived critical locus of a superpotential W) carries a 1‑shifted symplectic structure, and its quantization yields the B‑model topological string. The wall‑crossing formulas for Donaldson–Thomas invariants are interpreted as mutations in the derived Fukaya category, and the Kontsevich–Soibelman wall‑crossing formula becomes the statement that the product of quantum dilogarithms associated to spherical objects is invariant under derived equivalences. These results demonstrate that derived algebraic geometry is not merely a technical language but a crucial geometric framework for modern mirror symmetry.

  • Confusing the derived fiber product with the classical fiber product when Tor‑independence fails.
  • Assuming the virtual dimension equals the naive expected dimension without accounting for higher Tor groups.
  • Treating shifted symplectic and shifted Poisson structures as interchangeable without the degree shift.
  • Neglecting the hyperdescent condition when checking representability of a moduli functor as a derived stack.
  • Overlooking that Hochschild cohomology computes the tangent complex only after a degree shift by one.
  • Misapplying the derived Morita equivalence to categories that are not smooth and proper.
  • Forgetting that the quantization of a shifted Poisson structure requires an Ek+1‑operad, not just an associative algebra deformation.

Derived Critical Loci and (−1)-Shifted Symplectic Structures

Per Pantev–Toën–Vaquié–Vezzosi, the derived critical locus of a function f on a smooth derived scheme X — the derived fiber product X ×dCrit(f) X of the zero section and df — carries a canonical (−1)-shifted symplectic structure. The construction works for any f ∈ O(X) and yields a derived stack Crit(f) whose tangent complex at a point is the mapping cone of the Hessian of f. The (−1)-shifted symplectic form is induced by the canonical form on the shifted cotangent bundle T*[−1]X. When X is a classical smooth variety and f a regular function, truncating Crit(f) recovers the classical critical scheme, while the derived structure retains higher obstruction theories from higher derivatives of f. This framework underlies the mathematical definition of the B‑model topological string and the construction of virtual fundamental classes for Donaldson–Thomas invariants on Calabi–Yau threefolds. The shifted symplectic structure also yields a natural quantization via the E2-operad, producing a deformation quantization of the derived critical locus matching the physics of the topological B‑model.

Key properties

  • The derived critical locus is functorial with respect to morphisms of pairs (X, f).
  • The (−1)-shifted symplectic form is non‑degenerate in the derived sense: it induces an equivalence between the tangent and cotangent complexes shifted by −1.
  • For a Landau–Ginzburg model (X, W), the derived critical locus Crit(W) is the derived scheme of singularities; its category of singularities is equivalent to the derived category of matrix factorizations of W.

Derived Artin Approximation and Formal Moduli Problems

Derived Artin approximation (Lurie; Toën–Vezzosi) states that any formal moduli problem over a field of characteristic zero is equivalent to the formal completion of a derived algebraic stack locally of finite presentation. A formal moduli problem is a functor F : CAlgcnk → Spaces satisfying Schlessinger's conditions and a derived Rim–Schlessinger condition. The theorem identifies the ∞‑category of formal moduli problems with the ∞‑category of dg Lie algebras (or L∞-algebras) over k. Under this equivalence, the tangent complex of F at the base point corresponds to the underlying chain complex of the dg Lie algebra shifted by one. The proof uses the derived Artin approximation theorem for algebraic spaces and the fact that the ∞‑category of derived stacks is generated under colimits by representable derived schemes. Consequently, any deformation problem governed by a dg Lie algebra — e.g., deformations of a coherent sheaf, a perfect complex, or an A∞-algebra — is pro‑representable by a formal derived stack. This result foundations the derived geometric approach to moduli spaces: construct the formal moduli problem, apply derived Artin approximation to obtain an algebraic derived stack, then truncate to recover the classical moduli space with its virtual fundamental class.

Applications

  • Moduli of perfect complexes on a proper derived scheme: the formal moduli problem is controlled by the endomorphism dg Lie algebra RHom(E, E)[1].
  • Deformation theory of derived schemes: the tangent complex is the shifted tangent complex TX[1].
  • Derived mapping stacks: for a smooth proper derived scheme Y, the derived mapping stack Map(X, Y) is a derived Artin stack locally of finite presentation.
Worked Example: Formal Moduli of a Sheaf
Let X be a smooth projective Calabi–Yau threefold over ℂ and E a stable coherent sheaf on X. Describe the formal moduli problem of deformations of E and identify its tangent and obstruction spaces.
The deformation functor DefE sends a connective cdga R to the space of derived deformations of E over Spec R. By derived Artin approximation this functor is pro‑representable by the formal completion of the derived moduli stack MX of perfect complexes at [E]. The tangent complex at [E] is RHom(E, E)[1]. Its cohomology gives the classical tangent space Ext1(E, E) and obstruction space Ext2(E, E). Higher Exti (i ≥ 3) encode higher obstructions invisible classically but captured by the derived structure. The governing dg Lie algebra is RHom(E, E)[1] with the shifted Lie bracket from composition; its Maurer–Cartan equation reproduces the derived deformation equations.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for the tangent or obstruction theory of a moduli problem, first identify the governing dg Lie algebra (often an RHom complex shifted by one). Then state that derived Artin approximation guarantees pro‑representability by a formal derived stack, and that classical truncation yields the expected virtual dimension. Mention the (−1)-shifted symplectic structure on the derived critical locus if the problem comes from a superpotential.

Derived Azumaya Algebras and Brauer Groups

A derived Azumaya algebra over a derived scheme X is an algebra object A in the symmetric monoidal ∞‑category QCoh(X) such that A ⊗ Aop → End(A) is an equivalence and A is locally free of finite rank as an OX-module. Classically, Azumaya algebras classify Brauer group elements; in derived algebraic geometry the Brauer group is replaced by the derived Brauer space Br(X) = Map(X, BGL1(S)) with S the sphere spectrum. Toën and Antieau–Gepner–Heller show that the derived Brauer group fits into an exact sequence involving H2ét(X, Gm) and the topological Brauer group of the underlying space. Derived Azumaya algebras are precisely objects that become equivalent to matrix algebras after an étale cover in the ∞‑topos of derived stacks. This allows computation of Brauer groups of derived stacks such as the derived moduli of elliptic curves, where derived structure contributes higher homotopy groups invisible classically. Morita theory for derived Azumaya algebras implies the ∞‑category of modules over such an algebra is equivalent to QCoh on a derived Brauer‑Severi stack, giving a derived geometric interpretation of twisted derived categories.

Key results

  • The derived Brauer space classifies derived Azumaya algebras up to Morita equivalence.
  • For a connective derived scheme X, the map Br(X) → Br(π0X) is surjective with kernel given by higher cohomology of the structure sheaf.
  • Derived Azumaya algebras on a derived stack X correspond to Gm-gerbes in the étale ∞‑topos of X.

Derived Categories of Quasi-Coherent Sheaves on Derived Stacks

The ∞‑category QCoh(X) of quasi‑coherent sheaves on a derived stack X is the limit of QCoh(Spec A) over affine derived schemes mapping to X. When X is a derived Artin stack locally of finite presentation, QCoh(X) is a presentable stable ∞‑category compactly generated by perfect complexes. The tensor product makes it a symmetric monoidal ∞‑category with internal Hom given by derived Hom complexes. A fundamental theorem of Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum states that for a morphism f : X → Y, the pullback f* admits a left adjoint f! and a right adjoint f* satisfying ∞‑categorical base‑change formulas. The projection formula holds as an equivalence f!(F ⊗ f*G) ≃ f!F ⊗ G. These adjunctions are essential for Fourier–Mukai transforms on derived stacks and derived Bondal–Orlov reconstruction. In particular, if X and Y are smooth proper derived schemes with an equivalence QCoh(X) ≃ QCoh(Y) as symmetric monoidal ∞‑categories, then X and Y are equivalent as derived schemes. This extends classical reconstruction to the derived setting and underpins the categorical approach to mirror symmetry.

Technical points

  • Compact objects in QCoh(X) are precisely the perfect complexes.
  • The monoidal unit is the structure sheaf OX.
  • For a derived scheme X = Spec A, QCoh(X) is equivalent to the ∞‑category of A-modules.

Derived Geometry of Moduli of Sheaves and Bridgeland Stability

The derived moduli stack MX of perfect complexes on a smooth proper derived scheme X carries a natural (−1)-shifted symplectic structure when X is Calabi–Yau of dimension three. Bridgeland stability conditions on DbCoh(X) are a choice of slicing of the heart of a bounded t‑structure with a central charge Z : K(X) → ℂ satisfying the support property. In the derived geometric framework, a stability condition determines a good truncation of MX to an Artin stack of finite type whose points are semistable objects. The virtual fundamental class on this truncation is constructed using the (−1)-shifted symplectic structure and derived critical loci. Joyce and collaborators show the resulting generalized Donaldson–Thomas invariants satisfy wall‑crossing formulas given by the Kontsevich–Soibelman product of quantum dilogarithms. The derived enhancement is crucial: higher homotopy groups of mapping spaces in MX encode higher Ext groups controlling obstruction theory, and the shifted symplectic form provides orientation data for the virtual cycle. Brav–Bussi–Dupont–Joyce–Szendrői extend this to moduli of objects in a 3‑Calabi–Yau category, proving the derived moduli stack carries a (−1)-shifted symplectic structure and that the associated Donaldson–Thomas invariants are independent of stability condition up to wall‑crossing.

Outline of the construction

  1. Start with a 3‑Calabi–Yau dg category C (e.g., DbCoh(X) for a CY3).
  2. Form the derived moduli stack MC of objects in C; it is a derived Artin stack locally of finite presentation.
  3. PTVV provides a (−1)-shifted symplectic structure on MC.
  4. Choose a Bridgeland stability condition σ on C; this yields a truncation MCσ‑ss to an Artin stack of semistable objects.
  5. Use the shifted symplectic structure to construct a virtual fundamental class [MCσ‑ss]vir in the homology of the truncation.
  6. Define the DT invariant as the integral of 1 over this virtual class; wall‑crossing follows from variation of stability.
  • Confusing the derived critical locus with the classical critical scheme and forgetting higher Tor obstructions.
  • Assuming derived Artin approximation holds in positive characteristic without the characteristic‑zero hypothesis.
  • Treating derived Azumaya algebras as ordinary Azumaya algebras and ignoring higher Brauer group contributions.
  • Neglecting that QCoh(X) is compactly generated only for derived Artin stacks locally of finite presentation.
  • Applying Bridgeland stability to a derived category without a 3‑Calabi–Yau structure and expecting a (−1)-shifted symplectic form.
  • Overlooking that the virtual fundamental class depends on orientation data from the shifted symplectic structure.
  • These traps highlight subtle points examiners often test.

hand/string-theory.html:
Worldsheet Conformal Anomaly and the Critical Dimension

The Polyakov action possesses a classical Weyl symmetry that is broken at the quantum level by the conformal anomaly. The anomaly arises from the path‑integral measure of the worldsheet fields and is proportional to the central charge c of the two‑dimensional conformal field theory. For a free boson each coordinate contributes c = 1; for a free fermion each Majorana component contributes c = 1/2. The total central charge of the matter sector in the bosonic string is c_matter = D, where D is the number of spacetime dimensions. The ghost system introduced to fix the conformal gauge contributes c_ghost = -26. Vanishing of the total central charge c_total = c_matter + c_ghost = 0 forces D = 26, the critical dimension of the bosonic string. In the superstring the matter sector contains D bosons and D Majorana fermions, giving c_matter = 3D/2. The super‑ghost system (β,γ) contributes c_ghost = -15. The condition c_total = 0 yields D = 10. The anomaly cancellation is equivalent to the requirement that the Virasoro generators satisfy the quantum algebra [L_m, L_n] = (m-n)Lm+n + (c/12)(m3-m)δm+n,0 with c = 0 for the combined matter‑ghost system. This algebraic consistency underlies the absence of negative‑norm states and the unitarity of the S‑matrix.

BRST Quantization and the Physical State Condition

BRST quantization provides a covariant method to isolate the physical Hilbert space of the string. One introduces the nilpotent BRST charge Q_B = Σ_n c-n L_n^matter - ½ Σm,n (m-n) :c-m c-n bm+n: + … where c_n, b_n are the ghost oscillators and L_n^matter are the matter Virasoro generators. Nilpotency Q_B2 = 0 holds precisely when the total central charge vanishes, reproducing the critical dimension. Physical states |ψ⟩ are defined by the cohomology condition Q_B |ψ⟩ = 0 modulo BRST‑exact states |ψ⟩ ∼ |ψ⟩ + Q_B |χ⟩. At ghost number one this yields the familiar Virasoro constraints L_n |ψ⟩ = 0 (n>0) and (L0 - a) |ψ⟩ = 0 with the normal‑ordering constant a = 1 for the bosonic string, a = 1/2 for the NS sector, and a = 0 for the R sector of the superstring. The BRST formalism also clarifies the origin of the tachyon: the ground state of the bosonic string satisfies the physical state conditions but has negative mass‑squared M2 = -4/α'. In the superstring the GSO projection removes the tachyon from the BRST cohomology, leaving a supersymmetric spectrum. The BRST operator is essential for computing loop amplitudes, where the integration over the moduli space of Riemann surfaces is performed with the BRST‑invariant measure.

Worked Example: Central Charge Cancellation
Show that the critical dimension of the bosonic string is 26 by requiring the total central charge of the matter plus ghost system to vanish.
Each free boson contributes c = 1. For D spacetime coordinates the matter central charge is c_matter = D. The (b,c) ghost system of a conformal gauge fixing has central charge c_ghost = -26. The total central charge is c_total = D - 26. Setting c_total = 0 gives D = 26. This matches the requirement that the Virasoro algebra have no central extension in the combined system, ensuring nilpotency of the BRST charge and absence of negative‑norm states.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the critical dimension, write the central‑charge balance explicitly: c_matter + c_ghost = 0. For the bosonic string use c_matter = D, c_ghost = -26. For the superstring use c_matter = 3D/2, c_ghost = -15. This short derivation earns full marks and avoids memorisation errors.

Superstring Scattering Amplitudes and Modular Invariance

Perturbative superstring amplitudes are computed as integrals over the moduli space of super‑Riemann surfaces. At genus g the amplitude takes the schematic form 𝒜_g = ∫ℳ_g dμ ⟨∏_i V_i⟩ where V_i are vertex operators and dμ is the super‑moduli measure. The integration over the odd moduli is performed by picture‑changing operators, which shift the super‑ghost picture number and ensure the correct number of zero modes. Modular invariance of the torus (genus‑one) partition function is a powerful constraint: the one‑loop vacuum amplitude must be invariant under the SL(2,ℤ) transformations τ → (aτ+b)/(cτ+d). For the heterotic string this invariance forces the left‑moving bosonic coordinates to live on an even self‑dual lattice of rank 16, leading uniquely to the gauge groups SO(32) and E₈×E₈. At higher genus the measure factorises into a product of the super‑period matrix and the determinant of the Dirac operator; the cancellation of the chiral anomaly in ten dimensions is equivalent to the modular invariance of the genus‑one amplitude. The Green‑Schwarz mechanism, which adds a local counterterm to the effective action, is reflected in the worldsheet by the cancellation of the modular anomaly between the R‑NS and R‑R sectors.

Heterotic String Construction and Gauge Group Embedding

The heterotic string combines a left‑moving bosonic sector (26 dimensions) with a right‑moving superstring sector (10 dimensions). Sixteen of the left‑moving coordinates are compactified on an internal torus defined by an even self‑dual lattice Λ of rank 16. The momentum vectors p ∈ Λ satisfy p² ∈ 2ℤ, guaranteeing modular invariance of the one‑loop partition function. There are exactly two such lattices in 16 dimensions: the root lattice of SO(32) and the root lattice of E₈×E₈. The corresponding worldsheet fermionisation yields 32 left‑moving Majorana fermions λ^A (A = 1,…,32) with periodic (Ramond) or antiperiodic (Neveu‑Schwarz) boundary conditions. The GSO projection on the right‑moving side removes the tachyon and imposes spacetime supersymmetry. The massless spectrum contains the graviton, dilaton, antisymmetric tensor, and a gauge sector with adjoint representation of the chosen group. For SO(32) the gauge bosons arise from the 496 roots of the algebra; for E₈×E₈ the 496 roots split into two copies of 248. The heterotic string is a perturbative string theory that naturally yields a grand‑unified gauge group in ten dimensions, making it a prime candidate for phenomenological model building after Calabi‑Yau compactification.

M‑Theory on G₂ Manifolds and Phenomenological Implications

Compactifying M‑theory on a seven‑dimensional manifold X₇ of G₂ holonomy preserves N = 1 supersymmetry in four dimensions. The G₂ condition means the holonomy group of the Levi‑Civita connection is a subgroup of G₂, which is equivalent to the existence of a covariantly constant associative three‑form φ and its Hodge dual co‑associative four‑form *φ. The metric moduli of X₇ are parametrised by the cohomology groups H³(X₇) and H⁴(X₇); their dimensions b³ and b⁴ count the massless scalar fields (moduli) in 4D. Non‑abelian gauge symmetries arise from singularities of X₇: an ADE singularity along an associative three‑cycle yields a gauge group of the corresponding ADE type, with chiral matter localised at intersections of such cycles. M2‑branes wrapping associative three‑cycles give rise to particles whose charges are determined by the homology class of the cycle. The superpotential for the moduli is generated by membrane instantons (Euclidean M2‑branes) wrapping associative cycles, and by flux of the four‑form field strength G₄. Some G₂ compactifications can in principle produce the Standard Model gauge group SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1) with three families of quarks and leptons, but stabilising all moduli while obtaining a small positive cosmological constant remains an open problem. The swampland distance conjecture proposes that infinite distance limits in the G₂ moduli space are accompanied by towers of light states, which would constrain viable vacua.

  • Confusing the central charge of the (b,c) ghost system (-26) with that of the (β,γ) super‑ghost system (-15).
  • Assuming the critical dimension of the superstring is 26 instead of 10.
  • Neglecting the GSO projection when listing the massless spectrum of Type II theories.
  • Stating that T‑duality maps Type IIA to Type IIA; it actually exchanges IIA IIB.
  • Claiming that D‑branes carry only NS‑NS charge; they carry Ramond‑Ramond charge.
  • Believing that M‑theory has a fundamental string; its fundamental objects are the M2‑ and M5‑branes.
  • Overlooking that the heterotic gauge group emerges from an even self‑dual lattice, not from Chan‑Paton factors.

Worldsheet Supersymmetry and the RNS Formalism

The Ramond–Neveu–Schwarz (RNS) formulation introduces worldsheet supersymmetry by pairing each bosonic coordinate Xμ(σ,τ) with a Majorana fermion ψμ(σ,τ). The action in conformal gauge reads S = (1/2πα') ∫ d2σ (∂aXμ∂aXμ + i ψ̄μρa∂aψμ), where ρa are two‑dimensional Dirac matrices. The supersymmetry transformations δXμ = i ε̄ ψμ, δψμ = ρa∂aXμ ε close on‑shell into a translation. Quantisation of ψμ yields two distinct boundary conditions: periodic (Ramond) and antiperiodic (Neveu–Schwarz). The Ramond sector produces spacetime fermions because the zero modes of ψμ satisfy a Clifford algebra {ψμ0, ψν0} = ημν, generating a spinor representation of the Lorentz group. The Neveu–Schwarz sector has no fermionic zero modes and its ground state is a tachyon with mass2 = –1/2α'. The GSO projection removes this tachyon and enforces spacetime supersymmetry by keeping only states with odd worldsheet fermion number in the NS sector and a definite chirality in the R sector. In the heterotic string the resulting massless spectrum contains a graviton, dilaton, antisymmetric tensor, and a Majorana–Weyl gravitino with a dilatino, matching the field content of N = 1 supergravity coupled to super‑Yang–Mills. The super‑Virasoro algebra extends the bosonic Virasoro generators Ln with fermionic generators Gr satisfying {Gr, Gs} = 2Lr+s + (c/3)(r2–1/4)δr+s,0. The central charge c = 15 for the matter system (10 bosons + 10 fermions) cancels against the ghost contribution c = –15 from the (b,c) and (β,γ) systems, fixing the critical dimension to ten. The RNS formalism makes worldsheet supersymmetry manifest but obscures spacetime supersymmetry; the Green–Schwarz formulation reverses this trade‑off.

D‑Brane Boundary Conformal Field Theory

D‑branes arise as dynamical objects on which open strings can end. In the worldsheet description they are implemented by mixed boundary conditions: Neumann for directions tangent to the brane (∂σXa = 0) and Dirichlet for transverse directions (Xi = constant). The boundary state |B⟩ encodes these conditions in the closed‑string channel and satisfies (αnμ – Sμν α̃–nν)|B⟩ = 0, where S = diag(1,…,1,–1,…,–1) reflects the Neumann/Dirichlet split. The overlap of two boundary states yields the annulus amplitude, which by modular transformation equals the one‑loop open‑string partition function. This open‑closed duality is the worldsheet origin of the statement that D‑branes carry Ramond–Ramond charge. The massless open‑string excitations on a stack of N coincident Dp‑branes give a U(N) gauge theory with 16 supercharges, i.e. maximally supersymmetric Yang–Mills in p+1 dimensions. The low‑energy effective action is the Dirac–Born–Infeld (DBI) action SDBI = –Tp ∫ dp+1ξ e–Φ √(–det(Gab + Bab + 2πα'Fab)) plus a Chern–Simons term ∫ C ∧ eB+2πα'F that couples the brane to RR potentials. T‑duality along a Neumann direction converts a Dp‑brane into a D(p–1)‑brane, while along a Dirichlet direction it produces a D(p+1)‑brane. The boundary conformal field theory (BCFT) description also captures the dynamics of intersecting branes: chiral fermions localised at intersections can reproduce the Standard Model spectrum in many string‑phenomenology constructions. The Cardy condition ensures consistency of the open‑string spectrum by requiring that the annulus coefficients be non‑negative integers, which in turn forces the RR charge to be quantised.

Technique
A stack of three coincident D3‑branes in Type IIB string theory supports an open‑string sector. Determine the gauge group and the number of supersymmetries preserved by the low‑energy worldvolume theory.
The Chan‑Paton factors for N coincident D‑branes give a U(N) gauge group. For N = 3 the gauge group is U(3). A D3‑brane in Type IIB preserves half of the 32 bulk supercharges, i.e. 16 supercharges, which corresponds to N = 4 supersymmetry in four dimensions. The massless open‑string spectrum consists of a vector multiplet of N = 4 SYM with gauge group U(3). The U(1) factor decouples in the infrared, leaving an interacting SU(3) N = 4 theory.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for the gauge group on coincident branes, always start from the Chan‑Paton rule U(N) and then check whether an overall U(1) is projected out by the orientifold or by the GSO projection. Remember that the number of preserved supercharges is 32/2k where k is the number of independent Dirichlet directions relative to the bulk supersymmetry.

Flux Compactifications and Moduli Stabilization

Turning on background fluxes for the antisymmetric tensor fields is the primary mechanism for stabilising the geometric moduli of the extra dimensions. In Type IIB theory the relevant fluxes are the NS‑NS three‑form H3 = dB2 and the RR three‑form F3 = dC2. Their combined complex flux G3 = F3 – τ H3, where τ = C0 + i e–Φ is the axio‑dilaton, generates a Gukov–Vafa–Witten superpotential W = ∫X G3 ∧ Ω, with Ω the holomorphic three‑form of the Calabi‑Yau threefold X. The F‑term conditions DiW = 0 fix the complex‑structure moduli and the axio‑dilaton at supersymmetric minima. The Kähler moduli, which control the sizes of four‑cycles, do not appear in W at tree level and remain flat directions. Non‑perturbative effects such as Euclidean D3‑brane instantons wrapping divisors or gaugino condensation on stacks of D7‑branes generate a superpotential Wnp = Σ Ai e–aiTi, where Ti are the Kähler moduli. The combined superpotential W = Wflux + Wnp can stabilise all moduli in an AdS vacuum. Uplifting to a de Sitter vacuum is achieved by adding an anti‑D3‑brane at the tip of a warped throat (the KKLT construction) or by including D‑term contributions from magnetised D7‑branes (the Large Volume Scenario). The flux quantisation condition ∫Σ F3 = (2π)2α' m, ∫Σ H3 = (2π)2α' n restricts the allowed flux integers (m,n) and leads to a discretuum of vacua, often cited as a vast number (sometimes estimated around 10500 in specific constructions). The tadpole cancellation condition χ(X)/24 = (1/2κ102) ∫ H3 ∧ F3 + ND3 bounds the total flux and the number of space‑filling D3‑branes, ensuring consistency of the compactification.

Black Hole Microstate Counting in String Theory

The microscopic origin of the Bekenstein–Hawking entropy SBH = A/4GN for certain supersymmetric black holes is a celebrated quantitative success of string theory. The classic example is the five‑dimensional extremal black hole obtained by wrapping D1‑branes on a circle S1, D5‑branes on S1 × T4 (or K3), and adding momentum modes along S1. The low‑energy dynamics of this D1‑D5‑P system is described by a two‑dimensional (4,4) superconformal field theory living on the common circle. The central charge of the CFT is c = 6 Q1 Q5, where Q1 and Q5 are the D1 and D5 charges. The momentum charge Qp corresponds to the left‑moving excitation level NL = Q1 Q5 Qp. Using the Cardy formula for the asymptotic density of states, S = 2π √(c NL/6) = 2π √(Q1 Q5 Qp), which exactly matches the macroscopic entropy computed from the horizon area of the corresponding supergravity solution. The same method extends to four‑dimensional black holes in N = 4 or N = 8 supergravity, where the microscopic description involves D‑branes wrapping cycles of a Calabi‑Yau threefold or a K3 fibration. The topological string partition function computes the indexed degeneracies (the elliptic genus) which are protected by supersymmetry and can be continued to the black hole regime. The OSV conjecture relates the mixed partition function of BPS black holes to the square of the topological string amplitude. Recent developments using the quantum entropy function and localisation on AdS2 have reproduced exact microscopic degeneracies including subleading corrections for a broad class of supersymmetric black holes, confirming the holographic principle in a highly non‑trivial setting.

Swampland Conjectures and the Landscape

The landscape of string vacua is vast, but not every low‑energy effective field theory coupled to gravity can be completed into a consistent quantum gravity theory. The swampland program formulates criteria that separate the landscape from the swampland. The Distance Conjecture states that as one moves an infinite distance in moduli space, an infinite tower of states becomes exponentially light, with mass scale m ∼ m0 e–α Δφ. The de Sitter Conjecture asserts that the scalar potential V of any consistent theory must satisfy |∇V|/V ≥ c ∼ O(1) in Planck units, or alternatively min(∇i∇jV) ≤ –c' V, which strongly disfavors metastable de Sitter vacua. The Weak Gravity Conjecture requires that for any U(1) gauge theory with gauge coupling g there exists a particle of charge q and mass m such that q g ≥ m / MPl, ensuring that extremal black holes can decay. The Festina Lente bound relates the mass of a massive vector to the gauge coupling and the Hubble scale, m2 ≥ g2 H2, preventing parametric separation of scales in de Sitter. The No Global Symmetries conjecture posits that exact global symmetries are absent in quantum gravity; any apparent global symmetry is either gauged or broken by non‑perturbative effects. These conjectures are supported by extensive evidence from string compactifications, black hole physics, and AdS/CFT, but they remain unproven in full generality. They have profound phenomenological implications: they constrain inflationary model building, the viability of the Higgs potential, and the possibility of a cosmological constant that is both positive and parametrically small. Testing the swampland criteria against observational data is an active area of research at the interface of string theory and cosmology.

  • Confusing the central charge of the (b,c) ghost system (–26) with that of the (β,γ) super‑ghost system (–15).
  • Assuming the critical dimension of the superstring is 26 instead of 10.
  • Neglecting the GSO projection when listing the massless spectrum of Type II theories.
  • Stating that T‑duality maps Type IIA to Type IIA; it actually exchanges IIA IIB.
  • Claiming that D‑branes carry only NS‑NS charge; they carry Ramond–Ramond charge.
  • Believing that M‑theory has a fundamental string; its fundamental objects are the M2‑ and M5‑branes.
  • Overlooking that the heterotic gauge group emerges from an even self‑dual lattice, not from Chan‑Paton factors.

The advanced topics above form part of the core theoretical toolkit for modern string theory.

hand/schubert-calculus.html:
Equivariant Schubert Calculus and Torus Actions

Equivariant Schubert calculus refines ordinary intersection theory by incorporating the action of a torus T = (ℂ*)n on the Grassmannian Gr(k,n). The fixed points of this action correspond to coordinate subspaces, indexed by k‑element subsets I ⊂ {1,…,n}. The equivariant cohomology ring HT*(Gr(k,n)) is a module over the polynomial ring ℤ[t1,…,tn] (the equivariant parameters). Schubert classes σλ lift to equivariant classes σλT which satisfy a Pieri‑type rule with polynomial coefficients in the ti. The localization theorem of Atiyah‑Bott and Berline‑Vergne expresses any equivariant class by its values at the fixed points: σλT = ∑I (σλT|I) · [XI]T, where the restriction σλT|I is a product of differences tj−ti determined by the combinatorics of the Young diagram λ. This localization formula turns intersection numbers into rational functions in the ti, and the non‑equivariant limit (ti→0) recovers the classical Littlewood‑Richardson coefficients. Equivariant Schubert calculus is essential for computing Gromov‑Witten invariants with torus weights, for the study of quantum cohomology via the quantum equivariant Pieri rule, and for applications to the Horn problem on eigenvalues of sums of Hermitian matrices.

K‑Theoretic Schubert Calculus and Grothendieck Polynomials

In K‑theory the role of Schubert classes is played by the classes of structure sheaves 𝒪Xλ of Schubert varieties. The K‑theory ring K(Gr(k,n)) has a ℤ‑basis given by the (dual) Grothendieck polynomials Gλ(x) (or their stable versions). These polynomials satisfy a K‑theoretic Pieri rule: G1 · Gλ = ∑ Gλ+εi − ∑ Gλ−εj, where the sums run over adding or removing a box while staying inside the k×(n−k) rectangle, and the signs reflect the alternating nature of the K‑theoretic product. The structure constants cλμν in Gλ·Gμ = ∑ cλμν Gν are known to be non‑negative integers (the “K‑theoretic Littlewood‑Richardson coefficients”). They admit combinatorial descriptions via set‑valued tableaux (Buch) or via the Knutson‑Tao puzzles with an extra “K‑piece”. The Grothendieck polynomials also appear as representatives of Schubert classes in the connective K‑theory of flag varieties, and they specialize to Schur polynomials when the K‑theory parameter β is set to 0. The K‑theoretic Giambelli formula expresses Gλ as a determinant of the special classes G(p), mirroring the classical Jacobi‑Trudi identity but with binomial coefficients. These results are central for the geometric Satake correspondence in K‑theory and for the study of quantum K‑theory of Grassmannians.

Worked Example: Equivariant Pieri Computation
Compute the equivariant product σ(1)T · σ(1,1)T in HT*(Gr(2,4)) with torus weights t1,t2,t3,t4. Express the result as a linear combination of equivariant Schubert classes σλT with polynomial coefficients in the ti.
The equivariant Pieri rule for multiplying by σ(1)T adds a box to the partition λ; the coefficient for each term is a product of weight differences determined by the position of the added box (see, e.g., Knutson‑Tao or Molev‑Sagan). For λ=(1,1) in a 2×2 rectangle, the possible additions are: add a box to the first row (giving (2,1)) and add a box to the second row (giving (1,2)). Under a standard indexing convention, the coefficients become (t1−t2) for the first addition and (t1−t3)(t2−t3) for the second. Thus σ(1)T·σ(1,1)T = (t1−t2) σ(2,1)T + (t1−t3)(t2−t3) σ(1,2)T. Setting all ti=0 recovers the classical Pieri product σ(1)·σ(1,1) = σ(2,1) + σ(1,2).
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for an equivariant or K‑theoretic product, first write down the relevant Pieri‑type rule with the extra parameters (ti or β). Identify all valid box additions/removals inside the bounding rectangle. Compute the coefficient for each term by multiplying the appropriate weight differences (equivariant) or by applying the alternating sign rule (K‑theory). Finally, check the non‑equivariant limit to verify consistency with the classical Littlewood‑Richardson numbers.

Affine Grassmannians and the Geometric Satake Correspondence

The affine Grassmannian GrG = G(ℂ((t)))/G(ℂ[[t]]) for a reductive group G (e.g., GLn) is an ind‑variety whose T‑fixed points are indexed by dominant coweights λ. Its homology H*(GrG) carries a convolution product making it isomorphic to the representation ring Rep(LG) of the Langlands dual group LG. This is the geometric Satake correspondence (Ginzburg, Mirković‑Vilonen). Under this isomorphism, the intersection cohomology complexes ICλ of the Schubert varieties Grλ correspond to the irreducible representations Vλ of LG. The convolution product of IC sheaves matches the tensor product of representations, so the structure constants are the Littlewood‑Richardson coefficients for LG. For G = GLn, the affine Grassmannian contains finite‑dimensional Grassmannians Gr(k,n) as subvarieties in its components, and the Satake isomorphism recovers the classical Schur basis of symmetric functions. The affine setting also yields the “affine Schubert calculus” where the quantum parameter q appears naturally from the loop rotation action, linking quantum cohomology of finite Grassmannians to the homology of the affine Grassmannian via the Peterson isomorphism. This perspective underlies recent proofs of the quantum Littlewood‑Richardson rule and provides a representation‑theoretic framework for quantum K‑theory.

Combinatorial Models: Puzzles, Honeycombs, and the Horn Problem

Several combinatorial models compute Littlewood‑Richardson coefficients without tableaux. The Knutson‑Tao puzzle pieces (triangles with edges labeled 0 or 1) tile a triangular region; the number of tilings equals cλμν. The honeycomb model (Knutson‑Tao‑Woodward) represents the same coefficients as integer flows on a hexagonal graph, giving a piecewise‑linear description of the Horn cone — the set of possible eigenvalues of a sum of two Hermitian matrices with prescribed spectra. The Horn inequalities, originally conjectured by Horn and proved by Klyachko and Knutson‑Tao, are exactly the facet inequalities of this cone. These models extend to K‑theory (K‑puzzles with an extra piece) and to equivariant cohomology (puzzles with weighted edges). They also provide algorithms for computing quantum Littlewood‑Richardson coefficients by counting “quantum puzzles” that incorporate the parameter q. The honeycomb model has been generalized to other Lie types via the Berenstein‑Zelevinsky polytopes, giving a uniform combinatorial description of tensor product multiplicities for any reductive group. For exam purposes, it is crucial to recognize that the Horn problem (on eigenvalues of sums of Hermitian matrices) was resolved using the saturation conjecture (proved by Knutson‑Tao), which states that cNλ,NμNν > 0 for some N iff cλμν > 0.

Quantum K‑Theory and Motivic Schubert Calculus

Quantum K‑theory merges the quantum product (counting rational curves) with the K‑theoretic product (alternating sums of structure sheaves). The quantum K‑theory ring QK(Gr(k,n)) is a deformation of K(Gr(k,n)) over ℤ[[q]] whose structure constants are the genus‑zero, three‑point K‑theoretic Gromov‑Witten invariants. These invariants satisfy a quantum K‑theoretic Pieri rule (Givental‑Lee) where the classical K‑theoretic Pieri terms acquire q‑corrections corresponding to removing a rim hook of length n. The quantum Grothendieck polynomials Gλ(x;q) represent the Schubert classes in QK and satisfy a quantum Giambelli determinant. Motivic Schubert calculus goes further by replacing the coefficient ring ℤ with the Grothendieck ring of varieties K0(Varℂ) or the motivic stable homotopy category. In this setting, Schubert classes become motives of Schubert varieties, and the product structure encodes not only numerical invariants but also the geometry of the intersection loci. Recent work (Buch‑Mihalcea‑Richmond) shows that the motivic quantum Pieri rule involves classes of certain quiver varieties, linking Schubert calculus to the representation theory of quivers and to the cohomological Hall algebra. For competitive examinations, the key takeaway is the hierarchy: classical cohomology → equivariant cohomology → quantum cohomology → K‑theory → quantum K‑theory → motivic invariants, each step refining the previous by adding parameters (ti, q, β, motivic weights) and by replacing integer counts with richer algebraic objects.

  • Confusing the equivariant parameters ti with the quantum parameter q; they live in different rings and have distinct geometric origins.
  • Assuming K‑theoretic Littlewood‑Richardson coefficients are the same as classical ones; they differ by alternating signs and set‑valued tableaux counts.
  • Overlooking that Schubert varieties in the affine Grassmannian are indexed by dominant coweights without a level restriction, unlike the finite Grassmannian case.
  • Misapplying the honeycomb model to quantum coefficients without the extra q‑pieces; quantum puzzles require a distinct set of tiles.
  • Treating the motivic Grothendieck ring as a polynomial ring; it has non‑trivial relations (e.g., [ℙ1] = [𝔸1] + 1) that affect product computations.
  • Forgetting that the geometric Satake correspondence identifies convolution in homology, not cohomology, of the affine Grassmannian.
  • Neglecting the non‑equivariant limit check; it is the simplest verification that an equivariant or quantum computation is consistent with classical Schubert calculus.

These advanced topics illustrate how Schubert calculus connects representation theory, combinatorics, and enumerative geometry across multiple cohomology theories.

Schubert Calculus on Orthogonal and Symplectic Grassmannians

The isotropic Grassmannians parametrize linear subspaces that are isotropic with respect to a non‑degenerate symmetric or alternating form. For a symmetric form on a vector space of dimension 2n or 2n+1 one obtains the orthogonal Grassmannians OG(k,2n) and OG(k,2n+1); for an alternating form on a space of dimension 2n one obtains the symplectic Grassmannian SG(k,2n). Their Schubert varieties are indexed by strict partitions (orthogonal types) or by partitions whose diagrams fit inside a shifted staircase (symplectic type). The cellular decomposition by Schubert cells still holds, with each cell an affine space whose dimension equals the length of the corresponding Weyl group element in the appropriate Weyl group of type B, D or C.

The cohomology ring (with integer coefficients) is generated by the special Schubert classes σ_i subject to Pfaffian‑type Giambelli relations. For OG(k,2n+1) one has a presentation of the form H*(OG(k,2n+1);mathbb Z) ≅ mathbb Z[σ1,…,σk]/(σλ=0 if λ does not fit the shifted diagram). The Pieri rule for multiplying by a special class σr adds a horizontal strip of length r to the strict partition, with the additional condition that no two added boxes lie in the same column. The shifted Littlewood–Richardson rule of Worley and Sagan describes the structure constants; these coincide with the multiplication rules for Schur P- and Q-functions, linking the geometry to the representation theory of projective symmetric‑group representations.

Enumerative applications include counting isotropic lines on a quadric hypersurface, which can be expressed as a top‑intersection of the class σ1 on OG(2,2n). For low values of n the resulting numbers match familiar combinatorial sequences (e.g., the case n=3 gives 5 lines on a smooth quadric threefold). Similar counts in symplectic Grassmannians lead to analogous numbers, reflecting the parallel combinatorics of the two settings.

Degeneracy Loci and the Thom–Porteous Formula

Let E and F be vector bundles of ranks e and f on a smooth variety X, and let φ : E → F be a morphism of bundles. For an integer r with 0 ≤ r ≤ min(e,f) the r-th degeneracy locus is Dr(φ)={x∈Xmid operatorname{rank}φx≤r}. When Dr(φ) has the expected codimension (e−r)(f−r), its fundamental class in the Chow ring (or cohomology) is given by the Thom–Porteous formula [Dr(φ)]=Δ(e−r)(f−r)bigl(c(F−E)bigr), where c(F−E)=c(F)/c(E) is the formal quotient of total Chern classes and Δλ denotes the Schur polynomial associated to the rectangular partition λ=(f−r)(e−r). This expresses the class of a determinantal variety as a universal polynomial in the Chern classes of the bundles involved.

The proof proceeds by resolving the degeneracy locus via a sequence of Grassmannian bundles (the Fulton–Lazarsfeld construction) and applying the Giambelli formula for Schubert classes on the relative Grassmannian. The result is independent of the chosen resolution and holds in any oriented cohomology theory (Chow, singular cohomology, K‑theory, cobordism) after replacing Chern classes by the appropriate characteristic classes. In K‑theory the formula involves Grothendieck polynomials Gλ rather than Schur polynomials.

Applications include classical enumerative problems. For example, the number of lines meeting four general lines in ℙ3 can be obtained by interpreting the condition as a degeneracy locus on the Grassmannian Gr(2,4). The expected codimension is 4, and the Thom–Porteous formula yields the class σ1,12, whose degree is 2, reproducing the well‑known answer. More generally, the formula computes the class of loci where a section of a vector bundle drops rank, forming the basis of the Porteous–Kempf–Laksov approach to Schubert calculus.

Worked Example: Degeneracy Locus on Gr(2,5)
Let S be the tautological rank‑2 subbundle on Gr(2,5) and Q the quotient bundle of rank 3. Consider a general morphism φ : S → Q. Compute the cohomology class of the locus where φ has rank ≤ 1.
Here e=2, f=3, r=1. Expected codimension = (2−1)(3−1)=2. The relevant rectangular partition is λ=(f−r)(e−r)=(2)(1)=(2). The Thom–Porteous formula gives [D1(φ)]=Δ(2)bigl(c(Q−S)bigr)=c2(Q−S). Using the splitting principle, c(Q−S)=c(Q)/c(S). On Gr(2,5) one has c(S)=1−σ1+σ1,1 and c(Q)=1+σ1+σ2+σ2,1+σ2,2 (with standard conventions). Expanding the quotient and extracting the degree‑2 part yields c2(Q−S)=σ2+σ1,1. Thus the class of the degeneracy locus is σ2+σ1,1, whose degree is 2, meaning a general map S→Q drops rank at exactly two points on the Grassmannian.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks for the class of a degeneracy locus, first identify the bundles E, F and the integer r. Write down the expected codimension (e−r)(f−r) and the rectangular partition (f−r)(e−r). Then compute the Chern‑class polynomial Δλbigl(c(F−E)bigr) using the known Chern classes of the ambient variety (often a Grassmannian or flag variety). If the ambient space is a Grassmannian, express everything in the Schubert basis σλ and use Giambelli determinants to simplify. A quick sanity check: the degree of the resulting class must be a non‑negative integer; if it is zero, the locus is empty for a general map.

Schubert Calculus in Positive Characteristic and Frobenius Splitting

Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic p>0, Schubert varieties in the flag variety G/B (and in Grassmannians) are globally F-split: the absolute Frobenius morphism F:X→X splits as a map of 𝒪X-modules after restricting to any Schubert subvariety. Mehta and Ramanathan (mid‑1980s) showed that a compatible Frobenius splitting exists for all Schubert varieties simultaneously, using Bott–Samelson resolutions. A key consequence is the vanishing of higher cohomology of ample line bundles on Schubert varieties: for any dominant weight λ, Hi(X(w),mathcal L(λ))=0quadfor all i>0, where X(w) denotes the Schubert variety indexed by w∈W. This provides a characteristic‑p analogue of the Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing theorem and implies that the cohomology ring H*(G/B,mathbb Fp) is generated by the Schubert classes with the same integer structure constants as in characteristic 0, once Steenrod operations are taken into account.

Frobenius splitting also yields Kempf vanishing in positive characteristic: for a dominant weight λ, the higher cohomology of the line bundle mathcal L(λ) on the full flag variety vanishes. The argument uses the compatible splitting of the flag variety together with the exact sequence defining the line bundle. This vanishing is a crucial ingredient in proofs of the Borel–Weil–Bott theorem for large enough p.

In the cohomology H*(G/B,mathbb Fp) the Schubert basis forms a p-basis for the action of the Steenrod algebra. The cup‑product structure constants (the Littlewood–Richardson coefficients) remain the same integers as in characteristic 0 because they are obtained by intersecting reduced, irreducible Schubert varieties, a property that holds in any characteristic. However, Steenrod operations introduce additional relations; for instance, in H*(Gr(k,n),mathbb F2) the operation Sq1 acts non‑trivially on the class σ1, leading to mod‑2 relations useful for studying real Grassmannians via the Borel–Haefliger map.

Recent work by Brion, Kumar and collaborators extends Frobenius‑splitting ideas to quantum cohomology in positive characteristic, showing that the quantum product respects the splitting and that quantum Littlewood–Richardson coefficients retain the expected positivity properties. This suggests a coherent picture of quantum Schubert calculus over mathbb Fp, with the quantum parameter q treated as a formal variable in mathbb Fp[[q]].

Quantum Cohomology of Flag Varieties and the Quantum Chevalley Formula

The (small) quantum cohomology ring QH*(G/B) of the complete flag variety is a deformation of the classical cohomology ring over mathbb Z[[q1,…,qr]], where r=operatorname{rank}(G). The quantum parameters correspond to the simple roots (equivalently to the Schubert divisor classes σsi). The quantum product is defined by three‑point, genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants ⟨σu,σv,σw⟩d counting rational curves of degree d=(d1,…,dr) meeting three Schubert varieties. The quantum Chevalley formula (see Fulton–Woodward) gives an explicit rule for multiplying a quantum Schubert class σw by a divisor class σsi:

σsistar σw= Σ_{substack{α>0\ℓ(wsα)=ℓ(w)+1}} ⟨αvee,ωi⟩ σwsα + Σ_{substack{β>0\ℓ(wsβ)=ℓ(w)-⟨βvee,2ρ⟩+1}} qβ ⟨βvee,ωi⟩ σwsβ,

where the first sum records the classical Chevalley terms and the second sum records quantum corrections; qβ=∏ qi⟨βvee,αi⟩. Setting all qi=0 recovers the classical Chevalley formula.

Because divisor classes generate the classical ring, the quantum Chevalley formula determines the entire small quantum cohomology ring. It also leads to a quantum Giambelli formula: any quantum Schubert class can be expressed as a polynomial in the quantum divisor classes using the same determinantal expressions as classically, but with the quantum product. Buch, Kresch and Tamvakis used this to obtain a quantum Pieri rule for Grassmannians, where the quantum terms correspond to removing a rim hook of length n from the indexing partition.

The Peterson isomorphism identifies the quantum cohomology of G/B with the homology of the affine Grassmannian GrG after localising at the product of quantum parameters q=q1⋯ qr. Under this isomorphism, quantum Schubert classes correspond to homology classes of affine Schubert varieties, and the quantum product matches the Pontryagin (convolution) product on the affine Grassmannian. This perspective explains the observed positivity of quantum Littlewood–Richardson coefficients and connects quantum Schubert calculus with the geometric Satake correspondence.

  • Confusing the quantum parameters qi with equivariant parameters ti; they belong to different deformation rings.
  • Assuming the classical Littlewood–Richardson rule applies verbatim to quantum products; quantum corrections involve rim‑hook removal.
  • Overlooking that Frobenius splitting in positive characteristic requires the field to be algebraically closed and the variety to be globally F-split; not every Schubert variety splits in arbitrary characteristic.
  • Misapplying the Thom–Porteous formula when the degeneracy locus does not have the expected codimension; the formula describes the class of the scheme‑theoretic locus only under the expected‑dimension hypothesis.
  • Treating the quantum Chevalley formula as a simple sum over covering relations in Bruhat order; the quantum terms satisfy a specific length‑drop condition.
  • Neglecting the distinction between small quantum cohomology (only divisor classes deformed) and big quantum cohomology (all classes deformed); the Chevalley formula holds in the small ring.
  • Remembering that the Peterson isomorphism relates quantum cohomology to the homology of the affine Grassmannian, not its cohomology; the product structures differ (Pontryagin vs. cup).
